units.la: TRia sunt, si bene memini, VENCISLAE LAVINI, vir præstantissime, de quibus iudicium nostrum exquiris. Primùm rogas me, ut quo pacto quis exercere se possit in Anatome Physiognomica, quam in Organo nostro esse probauimus: Deinde, quo pacto principia illa Paracelsica, Sal, Sulphur, Mercurius, ad Methodum medendi à Galeno præscriptam accommo-dari possint. Postremò, ut quid sentiam de lapide illo philosophi-co tam multis, præsertim Arabi-bus & recentioribus decantato, paucis tibi aperiam. Equidem, si breuiter de his tribus ad te scri-psero, tria præcipua philosophiæ Paracelsicæ capita attigisse vi-debor. Quanquam autem non sum nescius, trium horum tractatio-nem, neque institui, nisi præpa-rato otio, neque paucis verbis absolui posse: tamen quæ vis est mei erga te amoris, in hac Epi-stola summa sequar fastigia rerum.
units.tr: There are three matters, if I remember rightly, Wenceslaus Lavinius, most excellent of men, on which you ask my judgment. First, you ask how a person may train himself in physiognomic anatomy, which we have shown to be in our Organon; second, how those Paracelsian principles, salt, sulphur and mercury, may be adapted to the method of healing prescribed by Galen. Lastly, you ask me to set out briefly what I think of that philosophers' stone so often celebrated by many, especially by the Arabs and more recent writers. For my part, if I write to you briefly on these three, I shall seem to have touched on the three chief heads of Paracelsian philosophy. Although I am not unaware that a treatment of these three can neither be undertaken without prepared leisure nor concluded in a few words, nevertheless, such is the strength of my affection for you that in this letter I shall follow the main heights of the matters.

units.la: ESse Physiognomica Anatomen: hoc est, Physiognomicae Anatomes doctrinam non esse fictū & commentitium quiddam: sed eiusmodi Anatomen esse in re & natura positam in Organo nostro, vt dixi, probauimus. Omnino est inconsyderati hominis exquirere rationes eorum quae non sunt. Itaque ante probandum fuit Physiognomicam Anatomen non esse commentitiam fabulam, quàm rationes inuestigādi τὰ συμπάσχοντα, καὶ ἀντιπάσχοντα exquireremus. Quod attinet ad Methodum inuestigandi τὰ συμπάσχοντα καὶ ἀντιπάσχοντα, haec in signis posita est. & quoniam Forma hominis, est Norma Formarum, non secus atq; Homo ipse est Dominus & Norma caeterorum Animalium: vt foeliciter in Anatome Physiognomica verseris, vniuscuiusque animalis terrestris etiā minimi, naturam, figuram, indolem, & affectus diligenter confiderare, omnésq; obferuationes ad Anatomē hominis tanquam ad Normam reuo care oportet: etiam initio facto à reptilibus, in quibus obscura est partiū distinctio. Neque verò aspernari debemus minima hæc quæ videntur.
units.tr: We have shown, as I said, that Physiognomical Anatomy is not some invented and fabricated thing, but that such an Anatomy is real and grounded in nature, in our own body. It is the mark of a careless person to seek the reasons for things that do not exist. So it had to be proved first that Physiognomical Anatomy is not a fictitious tale, before we sought the reasons for investigating what suffers together and what suffers in opposition [τὰ συμπάσχοντα, καὶ ἀντιπάσχοντα]. The method of investigating what suffers together and what suffers in opposition rests on signs. Since the form of man is the norm of other forms, just as man himself is lord and norm of the other animals, if you are to succeed in Physiognomical Anatomy you must carefully consider the nature, shape, disposition and affections of every land animal, even the smallest, and must refer all your observations back to the anatomy of man as to a norm. You should begin with the reptiles, in which the distinction of parts is obscure. Nor should we scorn these small things, which may seem trivial.

units.la: Διὸ δεῖ μὴ δυσχεραίνειν ϖαιδικῶς τὴν περὶ ἀτιμοτέρων ζῳῶν ἐπίσκεψιν. Ἐν ϖᾶσι γὰρ τοῖς φυσικοῖς ἐνέσί τι θαυμαστὸν, ᾗ καθάπερ Ἡράκλειτον λέγεταί ϖρὸς τὲς ξένες εἰπεῖν τὲς βελομένες αὐτῷ ἐντυχεῖν, οἳ ἐπειδὴ ϖροσιόντες εἶδον αὐτὸν θερομένον ϖρὸς τῷ ἱπνῷ, ἐσῄσαν. ἐκέλευσε γὰρ αὐτὲς εἰσιέναι θαῤῥεῖντας. εἶναι γὰρ κὴ ἐνταῦθα θεὸς. Οὕτω κὴ ϖρὸς τὴν ζήτησιν περὶ ἑκάσῳ τῆς ζῳῶν ϖροσιέναι δεῖ μὴ δυσωπεμένον, ὡς ἐν ἁπασιν ὄντος φυσικῆς κὴ καλῆς. τὸ γὰρ μὴ τυχόντως, ἀλλ' ἕνεκά τινος, ἐν τοῖς τῆς φύσεως ἔργοις ἐςὶ κὴ μάλισα. ὧν δ' ἕνεκα συωέςηκεν ἢ γέγονε τέλος τῶν τὰ καλῶ χώραν εἰληφεν. εἰ δέ τις τῶν περὶ τῆς ἄλλων ζῳῶν θεωρίαν ἀτιμον εἶναι νενόμικε, τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον οἴεσθαι χρὴ κὴ ϖεὶ αὐτῶ. κὴ ἐςὶ γὰρ ἄνευ ϖολλῆς δν χερείας ἰδεῖν ἐξ ὧν συωέςηκε τὸ τῆς ἀνθρώ-ϖων
units.tr: Therefore we should not be childishly repelled by the study of the less honourable animals. For in all natural things there is something wonderful. As is told of Heraclitus, when some strangers who wished to meet him came up and saw him warming himself at the oven, they hesitated at the door; he bade them come in without fear, for there too the gods were present. So too we ought to approach the study of each animal without distaste, since in all of them there is something natural and beautiful. For what exists not by chance but for some purpose is found most of all in the works of nature; and the end for which a thing has been made or has come into being holds the place of the beautiful. If anyone thinks that the study of the other animals is base, he must think the same of himself too. For it is not without great reward to see of what the human race is composed: blood, flesh, bones, veins and parts of this kind. [Aristotelis lib. 1. de partibus animalium] (Aristotle, On the Parts of Animals, book 1.)

units.la: Aristotelis lib. 1. de partibus animalium. πων γένος. οιον, αἱ μα, σάρκες, ὀστᾶ, φλέβες, καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα μόρια. Verba ipsa Aristotelis quin adscribere mus, non potuimus, tum propter elegantiam, tum etiam propter sententiarum diuinitatem. Quanquam autem, si Latinè reddere coner, mea interpretatione sententiarum maiestatem deterere videbor: experiar tamen vel ob hoc ipsum, quod apud Platonem praeclarè dictum legimus. Δὶς, τῇ τρὶς, τὸγε καλῶς ἔχον, ἐπαναπολεῖν τῷ λόγῳ δεῖν. Graua-tè ferre (inquit Aristoteles) puerorum more, ignobiliorum animalium consideratione no oportet. Nam in rebus naturalibus omnibus inest aliquid admiratione dignum. Proinde, quemadmodum memoriae proditum est. Heraclitum respondisse hospitibus ipsum conuenire cupientibus, qui cum accessissent, eumque cōspexissent in casa ad caminum se calefacientem, restiterunt, quippe iussit illos intrepide ingredi. Ibi enim deos quoque adesse praesentes.
units.tr: We could not bring ourselves to transcribe Aristotle's own words, both for their elegance and for the divine quality of their sense. Yet if I try to render them into Latin, I shall seem to diminish the majesty of his thought. I shall make the attempt nonetheless, if only for the reason that we read in Plato the well-said maxim: it is right to go over the argument twice, even three times [Δὶς, τῇ τρὶς, τὸγε καλῶς ἔχον, ἐπαναπολεῖν τῷ λόγῳ δεῖν]. Aristotle says that one should not take it hard, as children do, and be unwilling to consider the lesser animals, since in all natural things there is something worthy of wonder. Therefore, as is recorded in memory, Heraclitus answered the strangers who wished to meet him, who when they had come near and seen him warming himself at the hearth in his house, stopped; he bade them go in boldly, for the gods were present there too.

units.la: Sic etiam ad disquisitionem de vnoquoque animali nos accedere oportet, non stultè verecundantes aut cun ctantes: quippe in omnibus inest naturale quiddam & honestum. Nam non fortuitò, sed finis cuiusdam causa esse, idin naturæ operibus, vel maximè comperitur. Porrò Finis ille, cuius gratia res vnaquæque naturalis constituta est & codita, est instar boni & honesti. Quòd siquis existimat vilem & ignobilem esse cæterorum animalium consyderationem, is eodem modo de se statuat, necesse est. Neque enim sine multo & graui fastidio considerare queas, ex quibus humanum genus constat, cuiusmodi sunt, Sanguis, Carnes, Ossa, Venæ, & aliæ eiusmodi partes. Hæc Aristoteles. Quibus verbis mirum in modum commendat non solum hominis, verumetiam viliorum quoque animalium anatomen & consyderationem. Quapropter Aristotelis, Gesneri, & aliorum doctissimorum virorum rum lucubrationes mirum in modū nobis probantur, quibus animalium naturas persecuti sunt. Sed cognitio illa manca quodammodo, atque imperfecta est: nisi ad Anatomen homi nis, tanquam ad perfectionem referatur: nisi etiā accedat cognitio συμπαθείας stirpium & remediorum externorum. & vicissim cognitio stirpium, & externarum aliarum rerum manca atque imperfecta est: nisi cognitionem istam remediorum ex animalium anatome hauseris. Proinde claudicat Anatome, nisi sit gemina, siue duplex: Vna animaliū, quorum quidem Anatome, ad perfectissimi animalis, nempe hominis Anatomen reuocatur: Altera stirpiū & externorum remediorum. Ex illa Hominem morbi, (sic enim vocat Paracelsus ille alioquin impolitus scriptor sequutus phrasim Hebræam aut Arabicam,) hoc est morbum vnumquemque: Ex hac autem Fœminam, hoc est remedium, cognoscimus. Nullus affectus subsistere potest in nobis, inquit Ferneli, cui non pariter contrarium quiddam tanquam remedium Natura protulerit. Nullaque vsquam remediorum penuria, sed nostra eorum plerunque turpis ignoratio. Ac remedium in Anatome simile dicitur: quia habet Signa similia signis illis quæ sunt in homine morbi. Hinc etiam similes morbos, similibus curari: & contrarios morbos contrariis curari dicere licet: Ac similibus quidé curari: propter similia signa: Contrarius verò, propter Naturam contrariam cum morbo pugnantem. Quid breuiùs, quid rotundiùs, quid sapientiùs dici possit in consultationibus, quàm si medicus dicat, signìsque adhibitis demonstratione ꝯ probet, Hunc morbum esse illius remedij & remedium illud esse huius morbi? Vna proprietatum cognitio, inquit idem Fernelius, res ipsas exercet: Reliquæ omnes vix aliud quàm Verba. Quæ quum ipse mihi ante oculos propono, iam ferè anteactorum laborum me tædet, vehementérque pœnitet: idémque opto quod quod Euripides, vt res ipsæ cum hominibus colloquantur, & se, quales sint, explicent, vt procul amendentur artificiosi sermones.
units.tr: In the same way we ought to approach the inquiry into each animal, not hesitating or delaying out of foolish shame, since in all of them there is something natural and honourable. For it is found, most of all in the works of nature, that things happen not by chance but for the sake of some end. That end, for whose sake each natural thing is constituted and made, is like the good and the honourable. If anyone judges the consideration of the other animals to be base and ignoble, he must necessarily judge himself the same way. For you cannot consider, without great and serious disgust, what the human race is made of: such as blood, flesh, bones, veins and other such parts. Thus Aristotle. By these words he commends in a remarkable way the anatomy and study not only of man but also of the lower animals. Therefore the labours of Aristotle, Gesner and other most learned men are greatly approved by us, since they pursued the natures of animals. Yet that knowledge is in a way maimed and imperfect unless it is referred to the anatomy of man as its perfection; unless the knowledge of the sympathy [συμπαθείας] of plants and external remedies is added. And conversely, the knowledge of plants and of other external things is maimed and imperfect unless you draw that knowledge of remedies from the anatomy of animals. Therefore Anatomy limps unless it is twofold: one part of animals, whose anatomy is traced back to the anatomy of the most perfect animal, namely man; the other of plants and external remedies. From the first we learn the man of the disease (for so that otherwise crude writer Paracelsus calls it, following a Hebrew or Arabic idiom), that is, each disease; from the second we learn the woman, that is, the remedy. No affection can subsist in us, says Fernelius, for which nature has not likewise produced some contrary thing as a remedy. Nor is there anywhere a shortage of remedies, but our shameful ignorance of them is for the most part the cause. And a remedy is said to be similar in Anatomy because it has similar signs to those signs which are in the man of the disease. Hence we may say that similar diseases are cured by similar things, and contrary diseases by contrary things: similar things indeed cure through similar signs, but contrary things through a nature opposed to the disease. What could be said more briefly, more fully or more wisely in consultations than if the physician, with signs brought forward, should demonstrate and prove: This disease is of that remedy, and that remedy is of this disease? One knowledge of properties, says the same Fernelius, deals with the things themselves; all the rest are scarcely anything but words. When I set these before my eyes, I am almost weary of my past labours and heartily regret them, and I wish what Euripides wished: that the things themselves should speak with men and explain what they are, so that artificial speeches might be far removed.

units.la: Quid prodest tibi cognitio Nomenclationis stirpis alicuius, nisi etiam vim, naturámque eius cognoscas? At medici nostri vulgares magnificè se iactant atque ostentant designationibus partium corporis, stirpium, atque reliquorum remediorum, etiási naturas & vires minimè perspectas habeant. At ista Anatome mortua est. Nostra autem, quæ, vt dixi, gemina est, efficax & viua est, in qua res ipsæ cum hominibus colloquūtur, & se, quales sunt, explicant. Partes, ipsúmq; adeo corpus hominis mortui, dicuntur ὁμονύμως, partes & corpus, vt in philosophia demonstratum est. Os cadaueris, inquit Scaliger, caret ea forma, qua e- rat viuens. Caret etiam sine. Nullum enim eius officium, vt prius. Non est igitur idem. Quinetiam an eadem sit materia, dubitatū est in septimo Metaphysices. Neq; enim est, vt in arte factis. Vt eadem sit lorica, & vomeris materia, mutata forma. Nam si materia Cæsaris, non est materia huius equi, quia sub diuersis formis: non erit cadaueris materia eadem numero, quæ fuit viuentis. Longè enim magis distant, quàm materia Cæsaris, & huius equi. Hæc enim sub propinquiore sunt genere: quippe sub animali. Illa sub remotiore: nempe sub corpore. Hæc Scaliger. Addemus, non posse dici morbum inesse in cadauere. Ergo Anatome spectanda est in viuente animali quod morbo conflictatur. Consideranda sunt initia, considerandi progressus: hoc est, signa obseruanda & notanda sunt. Deinde signa similia perquirenda sunt in remediis externis. Nam remedium illud externum, quod similia signa geret, erit proprium remedium. At medici nostri vulgares dicent se perspectam habere remedii naturam, quippe norunt remedium esse aut calidum, aut frigidum, aut humidum, aut siccum: itemque quo gradu. Item perspectas habent secundas facultates, nempe faculfacultates incidendi, incrassandi, exasperandi, leuigandi, aperiendi, occludendi: rarefaciedi, densandi, &c. Respondebit Fernelius, Sapore multa aut profutura, inquit Fernelius, aut nihil certè nocitura putantur, quæ sæpe vidi taciti viribus: sola obseruatione noscendis, alia sumta, alia solùm admota, in perniciē summam & exitium miseros præcipitare. Vtinam qui omnem ætatem discendis stirpium nomenclaturis conterunt, operam suam iis experiundis sedulò nauarent. Hæc Fernelius. Quæ quum ita sint: perspicuum est multum operæ, multúmque studii ponendum esse in obseruatione & notatione signorum omnium, sine quibus Anatome gemina cognosci nequit. At quo pacto, inquies, tam multa signa, támque diuersa notabun tur? Nempe viam illam sequi oportet, quam in posteriore libro priorū Analyticœn tradidimus, in eo capite, quod est De Physiognomico syllogismo. Neque vnum aut alterū duntaxat signum colligendum est: sed συνδρομὴ signorum est cogenda, quæ reciprocè tum de morbo, tum etiam de Remedio dicatur. Sic medici etiā vulgares cogunt συνδρομὴν signorū. Verbi gratia, Pleuritidis: deinde signis omnibus coactis demonstrant ὅτι affectum istum esse Pleuritidem. Etenim si vnum aut alterum signum duntaxat adhibeatur, Verbi gratia, Febris assidua: Respiratio difficilis: Demonstratio ὅτι minimè constitue tur. Oportet enim in Demonstratione ὅτι, perfectam signorum enumerationem adhibere, nempe eiusmodi, vt cum causa διότι, & affectu ipso sit reciproca. Neque verò aliter colligenda sunt signa, quam quo modo colliguntur & notantur Antecedentia & Consequentia, ad medium Analyticum constituendum: de quibus Aristoteles in tractatu De inuestigandis principijs Syllogismorum omnium. ἡ μὲν ἐν ὁδὸς, inquit, κατὰ πάντων ἡ αὐτὴ, καὶ περὶ φιλοσοφίαν, ἢ περὶ τέχνλω ὁποίανἐν, καὶ μάθημα. Δεῖ γὰρ τὰ ὑπάρχοντα, ἢ οἷς ὑ-παρπάρχει, ὥσϵι ἕκαστον ἀθρεῖν, ἢ τέτων ὡς πλεί-ςων εὐπορεῖν:id est: Quare via hac eadem est in omnibus: in philosophia: in arte qua-libet & disciplina. Nam illa quae tribuun-tur,consiđerare oportet:& eiusmodi copiam quammaximam comparare.& paulò post. εἰ μηδὲν ἡγητὰ τῶ ἱστορίαν ἀφαλεῖφθείη, τῆ ἀλλη ἕως, ἡ ἀληθῶς ὑπαρχόντων ϖράγ-ματων:ἔξομεν ὥσϵι ϖαντὸς, ἃ μὴ ἔσιν ἀπό-δειξις, ταύτῳ εὑρεῖν ἢ ἀποδείκνυσι· ἐ δ' μὴ πέφυκεν ἀπόδει ξις, τῦτο ποιεῖν φανερὸν. Id est: Si nihil prætermissum sit ex illis, quæ obseruata sunt certò, & verè rebus inesse, licebit eius demonstrationem inuenire et proferre, cuius Demonstratio esse possit: illud verò, cuius Demonstratio esse non possit, licebit alia ratione manifestum reddere. Hæc Aristoteles. Sic etiam: Si nullum lignum prætermissum sit ex illis, quæ obseruata sunt, tum Homini morbi, tũ etiam Fœminæ siue externo remedio inesse: licebit Syllogismum Physiognomicum conficere, ex quo intelligamus hunc morbum esse huius remedij, & hoc remedium esse huius morbi: Verbi gratia: Tussilaginem esse Obstructionis pulmonum: & obstructionem pulmonum esse Tussilaginis. Sed Regis maximi opus est, efficere, ut multi docti viri, Physiognomicae Anatomes restituendae gratia, instituant συντήσεις: & in ea praestantissima doctrina sedulam seriamq; operam ponat.
units.tr: What good is it to you to know the name of some plant, unless you also know its power and nature? Yet our common physicians boast and show off grandly with the names of the parts of the body, of plants and of the other remedies, although they have not at all examined their natures and powers. But that Anatomy is dead. Ours, however, which as I said is twofold, is effective and alive, in which the things themselves speak with men and explain what they are. The parts, and indeed the body of a dead man, are said homonymously [ὁμονύμως] to be parts and body, as has been demonstrated in philosophy. The bone of a corpse, says Scaliger, lacks the form it had when living. It lacks even the name, for it has no function as before. It is therefore not the same. Indeed it is doubtful whether the matter is the same, in the seventh book of the Metaphysics. For it is not as in artifacts. If the cuirass and the matter of the ploughshare are the same, the form having changed: for if the matter of Caesar is not the matter of this horse, because they are under different forms, then the matter of the corpse will not be the same in number as the matter of the living body. For they are far more distant than the matter of Caesar and of this horse. These are under a nearer genus, for both are under animal; those under a more remote one, namely body. Thus Scaliger. We add that disease cannot be said to be in a corpse. Therefore Anatomy must be studied in the living animal which is struggling with disease. The beginnings must be considered, the progress must be considered; that is, the signs must be observed and noted. Then similar signs must be sought in external remedies. For that external remedy which bears similar signs will be the proper remedy. But our common physicians will say that they have a clear knowledge of the nature of a remedy, since they know that a remedy is either hot, or cold, or moist, or dry, and in what degree. Likewise they have a clear knowledge of the secondary faculties, namely the faculties of cutting, thickening, roughening, smoothing, opening, closing, rarefying, condensing, and so on. Fernelius will reply: Many things are thought either to be useful or certainly not harmful, which I have often seen by their powers in silence; by observation alone, some taken, others only applied, have plunged wretched men into the greatest ruin and death. Would that those who spend their whole life on the nomenclature of plants would devote their effort diligently to testing them. Thus Fernelius. Since these things are so, it is clear that much work and much study must be put into the observation and noting of all the signs, without which the twofold Anatomy cannot be known. But by what method, you will ask, will so many and such diverse signs be noted? Surely one must follow that path which we handed down in the later book of the earlier Analytics, in that chapter which is On the Physiognomical Syllogism. Nor should one or two signs alone be gathered, but a concurrence [συνδρομὴ] of signs must be assembled, which reciprocally applies both to the disease and also to the remedy. So even common physicians gather a concurrence of signs. For example, for pleurisy: then, with all the signs gathered, they demonstrate that [ὅτι] this affection is pleurisy. For if only one or two signs are used, for example continuous fever and difficult breathing, a demonstration that is by no means established. For in a demonstration that, one must use a complete enumeration of signs, of such a kind that it is reciprocal with the cause why [διότι] and with the affection itself. Nor must signs be gathered otherwise than in the way that antecedents and consequents are gathered and noted for constructing the middle term of the Analytic: concerning which Aristotle, in the treatise On discovering the principles of all syllogisms, says: "This way, then, is the same for all things, both in philosophy and in any art or discipline. For one must consider the things that belong, or to which they belong, so as to examine each thing, and must have as large a supply of these as possible." And a little later: "If nothing of those things which are truly observed to belong to things has been passed over, we shall be able to find and set forth the demonstration of whatever has a demonstration; and to make clear by another way whatever has no demonstration." Thus Aristotle. So too: if none of those signs observed has been passed over, then both of the man of the disease and also of the woman, that is, of the external remedy, it will be possible to construct a Physiognomical syllogism by which we may understand that this disease is of this remedy, and this remedy is of this disease. For example: that coltsfoot is of an obstruction of the lungs, and an obstruction of the lungs is of coltsfoot. But it is the task of a great king to bring it about that many learned men, for the sake of restoring Physiognomical Anatomy, establish collections, and devote careful and serious effort to this most excellent teaching.

units.la: DEinceps breuiter exponendū est, quo pacto tria illa principia Paracelsica, Sal, Sulphur, Mercurius, ad methodum medendi, & ad indicationes à Galeno in methodo medendi propositas accommodari queant. Ἐνδείξεις siue Indicationes propriè ex Anatome illa praestantissima, quam supra descripsimus, petendę sunt. Nónne, quaeso, res ipsae cum hominibus colloqui, & quales sint, per medicum explicare videntur, cum medicus cognitione verae Anatomes fretus, dicit, Hoc remedium esse huius morbi, & hunc morbum esse huius remedy? At medici nostri vulgares nullo syllogismo Phy- siognomico freti experimenta per mortes ducunt, vt cum Plinio lo-quar. Sed ad indicationes à Galeno propositas reuertamur. Tres summa indicationes medicatoria, inquit Gale-nus lib.19. Methodi med. cap. 13. su-muntur à morbo ipso, à corporis tempera-mento, & tertio nos ambiente aere. Hæ tres indicationes summæ, tria etiam indicant & commonstrant summo-pere obseruanda in methodo medé-di. Indicant enim Remedium: remedij quantitatem: & vtendi rationem. Nam morbus, siue sit similaris: siue Organi-cus: siue communis, remedium indi-cat. Temperamentum verò tum to-tius corporis, tum etiam partis indi-cat quantus sit recessus à pristino & naturali habitu: ex quo recessu intel-ligimus, quo pacto definienda sit re-medii quantitas. units.tr: Next, I must briefly explain how those three Paracelsian principles, Salt, Sulphur, Mercury, can be fitted to the method of healing and to the indications which Galen proposed in his method of healing. The indications [Ἐνδείξεις] are properly to be sought from that most excellent anatomy which we described above. Do not the things themselves speak with men, and show what kind they are, I ask, when the physician, relying on true knowledge of anatomy, explains through them? He says, This remedy is for this disease, and this disease is for this remedy? But our common physicians, relying on no physiognomic syllogism, lead their experiments through deaths, as I may say with Pliny. But let us return to the indications proposed by Galen. The three chief medicinal indications, says Galen in book 19 of the Method of Healing, chapter 13, are taken from the disease itself, from the temperament of the body, and third from the surrounding air. These three chief indications also point out three things that must be carefully observed in the method of healing. For they indicate the remedy, the quantity of the remedy, and the manner of using it. For the disease, whether it is similar, organic, or common, indicates the remedy. The temperament, however, indicates both of the whole body and of the part how far it has departed from its original and natural state; from this departure we understand how the quantity of the remedy is to be determined. To these two indications are referred those indications which are taken from the situation, seat and sympathy of the affected part, and likewise those taken from the time of the disease; these indeed show us the manner of using medicines. As for the surrounding air, an indication is taken from it for changing the climate, as when a pestilential plague rages, or certainly for correcting the air, and also for altering it, for example by heating or cooling it. But if anyone holds that true and living anatomy, he may be content with one indication, namely that which is taken from the disease, or from the sufferer of the disease, in which there are clearly signs altogether similar to those found in the external remedy. Thus Galen too, in the same book of the Method of Healing, namely chapter 15 of book 9, reduces all the indications to one. Now, as for those first three indications, says Galen, which we have mentioned, it is possible for you to reduce them to fewer, so that two of them, which indicate the cure, are altogether the heads: namely the present affection, which we call disease, and that which was before, which we have called health and natural habit. For healing itself is nothing other than the change of the present

Hæc Galenus. Sed Galenus videtur à Paracelso merito reprehensus, quòd mixtione, & crasi omnia remedia definiat, neglecta ipsa forma: cuius tamen, copellente ipsa veritate, multis in locis mentionem facere cogitur. Neque mirum esse aiunt, Galenum hæsisse in temperamentis, & qualitatibus: nempe in calido, frigido, humido, sicco: qui animam humanam, nihil aliud esse, quàm crasim multis in locis existimauit. Qua sententia, quid absurdius fingi possit, non video. Rectè igitur Paracelsus (inquiunt) calidum, frigidum, humidum, siccum, siue quatuor elementa, quæ vocantur, esse ait tanquam matrices rerum, in quibus per Anatomen illam magnam, veram & viuam remedia propria inuestigatur. Quinetiã rerũ naturaliũ cõpositarũ principia & confequętia summa, vir ille in alchimia ad miraculũ vsq; exercitat9, Mercuriũ, sulphur, & sale posuit. Quã quidẽ sententiã de principiis & cosequentibus summis, ne cui absurda videatur, multis huius sęculi experiętiis coprobari affirmat. Nã ex qualibet stirpe fit cinis: ex cinere sal: ex sale oleũ, siue sulphur & liquor, siue Mercurí9, qui neq; sal est, neq; flamma, queadmodũ sulphur cocipit. Et quoniã methodũ medędi tribus cõstitui diximus, remedio: remedy quantitate: & vtendi ratione, vt in istis tribus consequentibus summis, nempe in sale, sulphure, Mercurio, viuæ illius Anatomes propemodum immensæ, Epitomen ad remedia citò, & iucundè conferęda summopere necessariam habeamus: aiunt trium istorum naturas & proprietates diligenter & sigillatim in maiore mundo & in operationibus Chemicis esse obseruandas & inter se distinguendas: atque vna quidem ratione, ad remedium: altera vero ratione,ad vtendi rationem,tria ista consequentia esse reuocanda ad remedium. Tria ista reuocabuntur (inquiunt)sumta indicatione ab istis ipsis principiis morbos constituentibus, prout in corpore humano ista tria praeter naturam afficiuntur & mouentur. Porrò principia ista tria, quae sunt consequentia,non logica,sed in re posita & in natura vniuscuiusque rei compositae, moueri praeter naturam his fere modis. Primò quidem dicturi sumus de Mercurio (inquit Paracelsus lib. 2.Paramyrœn, cap. 4)Huc praedximus in homine liquorem esse,eúmque varium:unde & variae naturae ex ipso prodeunt. Verum nunc porrò sciatis, tres duntaxat in eo vias esse dissolutionis, quarum una est Mercurÿ eleuatio, quae dicitur destillatio:altera est sublimatio:tertia praecipitatio.Et aliquanto post, eodem cap. Hoc modo Mercurius, inquit,suo exstatu pellitur,vi caloris in exaltationem,quae nihil aliud est,quàm depulsio:quod est morborum veluti diximus, principium. Tres verò eius sunt modi. Vnus mortem subitaneam, eiúsque species efficit, quæ est destillatio. Alter gignit podagram, chiragram, & morbū articularem, quæ est Mercurÿ præcipitatio. Tertius facit maniam & frenesim, quæ est sublimatio Mercurÿ. Eodem in libro idem Paracelsus ait, Mercurium, hoc est, naturam primam, cerebri, medullæ, quam vocant, spinalis, & neruorum, de statu suo, hoc est, de suo temperamento, vt cum Galeno loquamur, calore deturbari, nempe quum factus est calidior, quàm par sit. Per se, inquit, hoc est, quum is in suo manet temperamento, sponte nihil istorum facit, sed necessariò aliquid extrinsece assumit, per quod ascendat, separétque se à reliquis duobus. Et paulò post: calor est, inquit, qui Mercurium de naturali gradu deturbat. Item: in homine, inquit, vel optimæ constitutionis, si cotidie se impleat, vel præter naturam se exerceat, aut talis ascensus, qualem diximus, contingat: cōmouetur totū corpus: hoc est, omnia eius membra incensa sunt. Vnde Mercurius conticōtinuè afcēdit ac descēdit, mouetúrq; vltro citróq; destillando in corpore, tanquā in pel-licano. Vbi autē peruenit in suum gradum, exercet suas nequitias: hoc est, postquam diu fuerit motus, adeóque subtilis effectus, (siue id fiat destillādo in corpore, siue præci-pitando, siue sublimando,) vt in suum ascen dat gradum, depellitur suo Astro, quod est corporis morbus & præsentissima mors. Item: Adeò fit subtilis Mercurius præpara-tione istiusmodi, vt nemo ipsi possit resiste-re, propter vim internā naturæ. Cuius iterū causa in promtu est. Sulphur, & sal non pos-sunt ipsum coercere propter vehementissimū calorē, qui repellit hæc duo. Ob id Mercurius adeò attenuatur, vt ossa & carnes penetret, non solùm poros, verumetiam alios in parti-bus, tanquam sudor, transit & penetrat: vt quùm afficitur, & acutissimus redditur in lue venerea. Hęc Paracelsus de Mercu-rio, hoc est, de prima natura cerebri, spi-nalis medullæ, & neruorum, in libro illo Paramyrœn. Quo quidem in li-bro videtur statuere, calore solo de suo statu Mercurium deturbari. Ait enim calorem Mercurÿ nimium, esse causam gra uissimorum symptomatum & asse-ctuum, vt Apoplexiæ, & aliorum e-iusmodi, Sic certè vinum largiùs & & sæpiùs sumtum, Mercurium exal-tat,tandemque gignit Apoplexiam, morbum articularem, & varias de-stillationes : At non calore solo, ve-rumetiam frigore, de statu Mercurius depellitur. Sic fiunt horror & rigor. Nã cum sanguis ad interiora confluat propter dolorem & afflictionem ner-uorum, fit, vt nerui refrigerati, frigo-risque molestiam percipientes, hor-rorem afferant: quemadmodum do-cet Galenus in libro De quatuor mo-tibus inuoluntariis. Quod si verba Pa-racelsi, licet impolita & inuoluta, ex-pendamus : comperiemus Paracel-sum quoque ipsum non aliter statuis se, quàm Mercurium frigore etiá de suo statu deturbari: verbi gratia, vt in horrore & rigore. Quemadmodum, in-quit,tam magno ascendit calore: ita quoque animaduertendum est, ipsum efficere varios rigores, horrores, & conquassationes, quoties eius paroxysmus incipit, aut aliqua tantum species. Quia subtile & acutum adeo venenum, quum innuadit naturam, ipsa incidit in quandam desperationem, sive terrorem, qui est corporis tremor prodiens ex metu & rigore. Et paulo post. Frigus, inquit, est materia & natura omnis timoris. Vbi autem calor vires accepit, frigus cedit calori, ut in paroxysmus febrium. Sic libro De natura quarto idem Paracelsus affirmat, Mercurium sive naturam cerebri & neruorum exteriorem, esse frigidam. Quod si ita est, vt est, non est mirum hydrargyrum, & quicquid frigidum est, esse neruis infestum. Vita Mercurij, inquit Paracelsus, nihil aliud est quam interior calor, & exterior frigiditas: hoc est, interius sui corporis calefacit, exterius frigefacit. Et merito vesti pellicea comparari potest, quae etiam, ut Mercurius, calefacit & frigefacit. Nam si vestis pellicea pars interior & pilosa nudo corpori applicetur, calefacit. Sin parte glabra, quam exteriorem appellamus, corpori nudo applicata vestis gestetur, frigefacit,& valet contra nimium calorem. Hæc Paracelsus de Mercurio, hoc est de natura illa prima cerebri, medullæ spinalis,& neruorum. Rursus ex multis,quæ de sale,hoc est, de prima illa natura iecoris, venarum, & sanguinis tradidit, pauca depromemus. Sic enim ex illis incultis Myrotheciis, quasi de stercore, aurum colligemus. Notandum est,inquit Paracelsus,salem mutari,resolutione, calcinatione, reuerberatione, & alcalisatione, & aliquanto post. Calor, inquit, multis de causis non relinquit salem resolutum in corpore, sed eũ expellit:nec solũ sale resolutũ expellit, verùetiã reliquos sales calcinatos & reuerberatos. Vnde sudor salsus existit,qui nihil aliud est quã sal resolutus. Hinc sequitur aliossudores ex sanguine,alios ex carne, vel ossibus, vel medulla,vel alia parte aliqua corporis prodire. units.tr: affection of the vitiated state into the natural habit. Since these affections are contraries, the transfer of one into the other must be made through contraries. And so again the one most general indication of cures will be contrariety. Thus Galen. But Galen seems to have been rightly criticised by Paracelsus, because he defines all remedies by mixture and crasis, neglecting form itself, though under pressure from truth itself he is compelled to mention form in many places. They say it is no wonder that Galen clung to temperaments and qualities, namely the hot, cold, moist and dry, and that he thought in many places that the human soul is nothing other than a crasis. I do not see what more absurd opinion could be invented. Rightly, then, (they say) Paracelsus says that the hot, cold, moist and dry, or the four elements as they are called, are like the matrices of things, in which proper remedies are sought through that great, true and living anatomy. Moreover, the principles and highest consequences of composite natural things, Mercury, sulphur, and salt, were laid down by that man, who was trained in alchemy to a wonderful degree. He affirms that this opinion about the principles and highest consequences, lest it seem absurd to anyone, is confirmed by many experiences of this age. For from any plant ash is made; from ash salt; from salt oil, or sulphur and liquor, or Mercury, which is neither salt nor flame, as sulphur conceives. And since we said that the method of healing is constituted by three things, the remedy, the quantity of the remedy, and the manner of using it, so that, in these three highest consequences, namely salt, sulphur, Mercury, we have a summary, very necessary for quickly and pleasantly bringing remedies together, of that living anatomy which is almost immeasurable: they say that the natures and properties of these three are to be observed and distinguished from one another carefully and separately in the greater world and in chemical operations; and that by one reasoning these three consequences are to be referred to the remedy, and by another reasoning to the manner of using it. These three will be referred back (they say), taking the indication from those very principles that constitute diseases, as these three are affected and moved in the human body contrary to nature. Moreover, these three principles, which are consequences not logically but in the thing posited and in the nature of each composite thing, are moved contrary to nature in roughly these ways. First, indeed, we shall speak of Mercury (says Paracelsus, book 2 of the Paramyrum, chapter 4): I have said above that there is a liquid in man, and it is various, whence various natures proceed from it. But now know further that there are only three ways of dissolution in it: one is the elevation of Mercury, which is called distillation; another is sublimation; the third is precipitation. And a little later, in the same chapter: In this way Mercury, he says, is driven from its state by the force of heat into exaltation, which is nothing other than expulsion: this is, as we have said, the principle of diseases. Its modes are three. One produces sudden death and its kinds, which is distillation. Another begets gout, chiragra, and articular disease, which is the precipitation of Mercury. The third produces mania and frenzy, which is the sublimation of Mercury. In the same book Paracelsus says that Mercury, that is, the first nature of the brain, of what they call the spinal marrow, and of the nerves, is deranged from its state, that is, from its temperament, to use Galen's words, by heat, namely when it has become hotter than it should be. Of itself, he says, that is, when it remains in its own temperament, it does none of these things spontaneously, but necessarily takes something from outside through which it may rise and separate itself from the other two. And a little later: It is heat, he says, that drives Mercury from its natural degree. Again: In man, he says, even of the best constitution, if he fills himself every day, or exerts himself contrary to nature, or such an ascent as we have described occurs, the whole body is stirred: that is, all its members are set on fire. Hence Mercury continually rises and falls, and is moved to and fro by distilling in the body, as in a pelican. But when it reaches its degree, it exercises its wickedness: that is, after it has been moved for a long time and has become so subtle (whether this happens by distilling in the body, or by precipitating, or by sublimating), that it rises to its degree, it is driven out by its own star, which is disease of the body and most present death. Again: Mercury becomes so subtle by such preparation that no one can resist it, on account of the internal power of its nature. The cause of this is again ready at hand. Sulphur and salt cannot restrain it, on account of the most vehement heat which repels these two. For this reason Mercury is so attenuated that it penetrates bones and flesh, and passes and penetrates not only the pores but also other parts, like sweat; and when it is affected it becomes most acute in venereal pox. These are the words of Paracelsus about Mercury, that is, about the first nature of the brain, spinal marrow, and nerves, in that book Paramyrum. In that book he seems to hold that Mercury is driven from its state by heat alone. For he says that excessive heat of Mercury is the cause of the gravest symptoms and affections, such as apoplexy and others of that kind. Certainly wine taken more freely and more often exalts Mercury and at last begets apoplexy, articular disease, and various distillations. But Mercury is driven from its state not by heat alone but also by cold. Thus chills and shivering arise. For when blood flows to the inner parts because of the pain and affliction of the nerves, it happens that the nerves, cooled and perceiving the discomfort of cold, bring on shivering, as Galen teaches in his book On the Four Involuntary Motions. If we weigh the words of Paracelsus, though rough and obscure, we shall find that Paracelsus himself also holds nothing other than that Mercury is driven from its state by cold as well, for example in shivering and chill. As he has risen with such great heat, he says, so it must be noticed that it produces various chills, shivers and shakings whenever its paroxysm begins, or some kind of it. Since the poison is so subtle and sharp, when it attacks the nature, the nature falls into a certain despair or terror, which is a trembling of the body arising from fear and cold. And a little later: Cold, he says, is the matter and nature of all fear. But when heat has gained strength, cold yields to heat, as in the paroxysm of fevers. So too in the fourth book of De natura Paracelsus affirms that Mercury, or the outer nature of the brain and nerves, is cold. If this is so, as it is, it is no wonder that quicksilver, and whatever is cold, is hostile to the nerves. The life of Mercury, he says, is nothing other than inner heat and outer coldness: that is, it warms its body inwardly and cools it outwardly. And rightly a fur coat can be compared to it, which, like Mercury, both warms and cools. For if the inner, hairy part of a fur coat is applied to the naked body, it warms; but if the smooth part, which we call outer, is applied to the naked body and worn, it cools and resists excessive heat. These are the words of Paracelsus about Mercury, that is, about that first nature of the brain, spinal marrow, and nerves. Again, from the many things he handed down about salt, that is, about that first nature of the liver, veins, and blood, I shall bring forth a few. For thus from those untilled dunghills, as it were from dung, we shall gather gold. It is to be noted, says Paracelsus, that salt is changed by dissolution, calcination, reverberation, and alkalisation, and a little later: Heat, he says, for many reasons does not leave salt dissolved in the body, but expels it; and it expels not only dissolved salt but also the other calcined and reverberated salts. Hence salty sweat arises, which is nothing other than dissolved salt. Hence it follows that some sweats come forth from blood, others from flesh, or bones, or marrow, or some other part of the body. It also follows that these salts have various natures, since from them arise creeping eruptions, pustules, itching, scabies, and other things of the same kind, which are described in surgery. Again, salts, he says, are then calcined when they have lost their liquid

units.tr: Paramy. eod. lib. c.5. They lose it. For thus the calcined salt lies, like alum in its preparation, or vitriol, or something else. And a little later: When the salt is no longer as moist as it ought to be, it presses outward and, by gnawing, opens passages for itself, and finds a way out at the part of the body where it lies. Likewise: What is reverberated, he says, is another salt: namely, a liquid, moist salt, which, dripping in its own distillation, moves apart, and this is properly what is called reverberation. And just as oil and water cannot be mixed, so no other substance passes into the substance of this salt. Its spirits therefore are carried back and forth, up and down, until a mucilage, or viscosity, is formed. For then it becomes far sharper than it should be and goes forth: that is, the internal heat drives its substance outward, and it begins to gnaw passages and produces other external disorders. You will note, therefore, that the salt tends whither its nature leads it, whence many diseases spring up, which in surgery I call ulcerous wounds. And a little later: From this it is understood how salt varies, now in this way, now in that. Whence come dry, moist, flowing, purulent disorders, etc. Paracelsus sets out these and many other things about salt in the second book of the Paramyrum, chapter five. Lastly, from the many things that he teaches about sulphur, that is, about the primary nature of the heart and arteries, in chapter six of the same book, the same Paracelsus, we have chosen a few, so that we may understand how sulphur too is moved and produces diseases through intemperance. The four Elements, he says, are four craftsmen, who turn sulphur into its transmutation, so that it departs from its office in generating diseases: of which many kinds arise, one cold, another moist, another dry; and again, within each kind many species arise, according to the nature of the matter of sulphur, which is found in its own regions and members, etc. These are Paracelsus's words; and in the second book of the Paramyrum he says much more about sulphur. We grant that Paracelsus, carried away by the madness [ἐρωμανίᾳ] of alchemy, abused these principles, their kingdom and their licence, for everything. But what, his followers say, would he have done, since more convenient names have not yet been found, and perhaps cannot be found? If the things themselves are placed in nature as they are, let us not reject these names too fastidiously and childishly, but keep them until they find more convenient appellations. In Theodorus Ducas Lascaris, in his books On natural communication, these principles are designated by three letters, and the four qualities by as many letters, as we are assured. Let us return to the indications [Εὐδαιμονίας], or indications. According to Galen, two highest and principal indications are constituted: the disease and the temperament. But when we name the disease, Paracelsus's followers do not wish the cause of the same kind [ὁμόγονον] to be passed over. For the disease, they say, is not removed unless the cause is removed. Hence it is also a wonder to the same men what came into Galen's mind, who made no mention of any cause of the similar parts [ὁμοιομερῶν], when he set out the three highest kinds of diseases from which the indications of remedies are sought. As if someone should promise to teach an art by which diseases are removed, and then not teach where the things necessary for that purpose can be obtained, but offer a great number of diseases of every kind. Now a cause of the same kind [ὁμόγονος] (as Aristotle teaches, in the second book of the Posterior Analytics, chapter 11) is one that never leaves its effect unaccompanied. Let the subject be water. Let the attribute be congealed. Let the middle term, or cause of the same kind [ὁμόγονος], be the absence of all heat. The cause is of the same kind [ὁμόγονος] because it abandons that of which it is the cause neither in the present, nor in the past, nor in the future tense. For ice is made when there is an absence of all heat. Ice has come to be when there was, or has come to be, an absence of all heat. Ice will be when there will be an absence of all heat. So in the science of healing, they say, the causes of the same kind [ὁμόγονοι] are these: Salt, Sulphur, Mercury, when they are thrown down from their natural state. Salt is that which is made from ash. From any compound thing ash is made. Therefore from any thing salt is made. Salt. But sulphur is everything that catches fire in the manner of oil and sulphur. Mercury is the name of that liquor, or spirit, which, having neither the nature of salt nor of sulphur, flees fire. Again, they say, salt is proper to the liver, which indeed is the most excellent organ of the lower belly. Likewise, because of the liver, it is proper to the veins, which, proceeding from the liver, are distributed to all parts of the body: so that salt agrees with all parts of the body for no other reason than that they share in the veins and blood. Sulphur, or oil, properly belongs to the middle cavity, that is, to the thorax, on account of the heart, and then to the other parts of the body through the arteries which are led from the heart into the body. That most refined Mercury properly belongs to the animal spirit, which is in the brain, and in that highest cavity of the head as in a citadel; and accordingly, through the nerves, to the other parts of the body that share in the nerves. But of these things we shall also speak below, when we set out the manner of using them.

units.la: {a}liceatur artem traditurum, qua mor- bi tollantur: ac postea, non unde pa-rari possint, quae ad eam rem sunt necessaria, doceat: sed magnum morborum omnis generis numerū proferat. Est autem causa ὁμόγονος, (vt docet Aristoteles, lib.2. posteriorum Analyt. cap.11.) quae nullo tempore incomitatum relinquit illud cuius est causa. Esto subiectum, aqua. Attributum esto, concreta. Medium siue causa ὁμόγονος, esto, vacuitas omnis caloris. Est ὁμόγονος causa haec: quia neque praesenti, neque praeterito, neque futuro tempore deserit illud cuius est causa. Nam fit glacies: quum fit vacuitas ab omni calore. Extitit glacies, quum fuit, siue extitit vacuitas ab omni calore. Erit glacies, quum erit vacuitas ab omni calore. Sic in medendi scientia, inquiunt, causae ὁμόγονοι sunt hae: Sal, Sulphur, Mercurius, quum a suo statu naturali deturbantur. Sal est ille, qui fit ex cinere. Ex qualibet re composita fit cinis. Ergo ex qualibet re fit sal. sal. At sulphur est illud omne, quod olei & sulphuris more flammam concipit. Mercurius appellatur liquor ille, siue spiritus qui neque salis, neque sulphuris naturam habens, ignem fugit. Rursus sal, inquiunt, est proprius iecoris, quod quidem iecur est inferi ventris praestatissimum viscus. Idem propter iecur, est proprius venarum, quae a iecore profectae, distribuuntur in omnes partes corporis: adeo vt sal non alia ratione conueniat omnibus corporis partibus, quam qua sunt venarū & sanguinis participes. sulphur, siue oleum mediae capacitati, id est Thoraci, propter cor, proprie conuenit, ac caeteris deinde corporis partibus, per arterias, quae a corde in corpus diducuntur. Mercurius ille elaboratissimus, spiritui animali, qui est in cerebro, & in summa illa capacitate capitis tanquam in arce, proprie conuenit: ac proinde per neruos, caeteris corporis partibus, quae neruorū sunt participes. Sed de his infra etiam di-
units.tr: promises to teach the art by which diseases are cured, and afterwards does not teach where the things necessary for that purpose may be obtained, but sets out a great number of diseases of every kind. Now a homogonous cause [ὁμόγονος] (as Aristotle teaches, in the second book of the Posterior Analytics, ch. 11) is one that never leaves the thing of which it is the cause unaccompanied at any time. Let the subject be water. Let the attribute be congealed. Let the middle, or homogonous cause, be the absence of all heat. It is a homogonous cause because it deserts the thing of which it is the cause neither in the present, nor in the past, nor in the future tense. For ice comes to be when there is an absence of all heat. Ice has come to be, since there was, or has been, an absence of all heat. Ice will be when there will be an absence of all heat. Thus, they say, in the science of healing the homogonous causes are these: Salt, Sulphur, Mercury, when they are knocked out of their natural state. Salt is that which is made from ash. From any compound thing ash is made. Therefore from any thing salt is made. Sulphur is all that which catches fire in the manner of oil and sulphur. Mercury is that liquid, or spirit, which has neither the nature of salt nor of sulphur, and which shuns fire. Again, they say, salt belongs properly to the liver, which is the most excellent viscus of the lower belly. Likewise, on account of the liver, it belongs properly to the veins, which proceed from the liver and are distributed to all parts of the body; so that salt agrees with all parts of the body in no other way than in that they share in the veins and the blood. Sulphur, or oil, belongs properly to the middle cavity, that is, the chest, on account of the heart, and then to the other parts of the body through the arteries, which are led from the heart into the body. That most refined Mercury belongs properly to the animal spirit, which is in the brain and in the highest cavity of the head as in a citadel; and accordingly it reaches the other parts of the body through the nerves, which share in the nerves. But we shall speak of these things further below, when we set out the method of using them.

units.la: cemus,quum vtendi rationem expo nemus.His tribus,nempe sale,sulphu-re,mercurio, corpus nostrum primùm constitui affirmant.Sic Fernelius lib. 7. physiologiæ, qui est de hominis procreatione,cap. 9. tres bullas in medio femine constitui ait, quasi guttas pellucidas, quæ rudimeta exhibent trium principiorum, iecoris, cordis,& cerebri. Quod attinet ad quatuor illa vulgata principia,sanguine, vtramque bilem,& pituitam: affirmant vnum sanguinem, quippe qui naturam salis adhibeat, principium esse: vtramque bilem, & pituitam excrementa esse ipsis principiis posteriora. Neque bilem vtramque, pituitam posse commodè coniugari cum qualitatibus illis primis:hoc est, cum calido,frigido,humido,sicco. At prin cipia ista tria,salem, sulphur,mercurium, cum qualitatibus illis primis cómodissimè aptissimèque coniugari posse. Atque ista omnia accuratissimè à nobis demonstrata esse apud Theodorum dorum Ducam Lascarim in libris De communicatione naturali.Quoties enim, inquiunt, principia tria hæc de suo statu deturbantur: cum qualitatibus illis extra modum & naturam siue temperamentum excedentibus, coniugentur necesse est, his fermè modis. Sal est, aut calidior, aut frigidior, aut humidior, aut siccior. Item, Sulphur est aut calidius, aut frigidius, aut humidius, aut siccius. Item, Mercurius est aut calidior, aut frigidior, aut humidior, aut siccior. Ex quibus perspicuè intelligi aiunt, semper vtendum esse comparatione, quoties qualitates in his principiis spectatur, quâ à temperamento & à natura discesserunt. Galenus igitur, inquiunt, quum morbos similares enumerat, qualitates à temperamento & à natura discedentes, hoc est, συντομίας considerat neglectis tribus principiis. At Paracelsi sectatores tria ista principia, non sine grauissimo vniuersæ medicinæ damno, prætermitti affirmant. Sic etiam eadem hæc prin
units.tr: These three, namely salt, sulphur, mercury, they affirm first constitute our body. Thus Fernel, in the seventh book of his Physiology, which is on the procreation of man, ch. 9, says that three bubbles are formed in the middle of the seed, like transparent drops, which exhibit the rudiments of three principles: of the liver, of the heart, and of the brain. As for those four commonly accepted principles, blood, both biles, and phlegm: they affirm that blood alone, since it has the nature of salt, is a principle, and that both biles and phlegm are excrements, later than the principles themselves. Nor can both biles and phlegm be conveniently joined with those first qualities, that is, with hot, cold, moist, dry. But those three principles, salt, sulphur, mercury, can be joined with those first qualities most conveniently and most aptly. And all these things, they say, have been demonstrated by us most accurately in the books of Theodore Ducas Lascaris On natural communication. For whenever, they say, these three principles are knocked out of their state, they must necessarily be joined with those qualities that exceed the measure and nature, or temperament, in roughly these ways: Salt is either hotter, or colder, or moister, or drier. Likewise, Sulphur is either hotter, or colder, or moister, or drier. Likewise, Mercury is either hotter, or colder, or moister, or drier. From which, they say, it is clearly understood that a comparison must always be used whenever the qualities in these principles are examined, by which they have departed from temperament and from nature. Galen therefore, they say, when he enumerates the similar diseases, considers the qualities departing from temperament and from nature, that is, he treats them briefly [συντομίας], having neglected the three principles. But the followers of Paracelsus affirm that those three principles are passed over, not without the most serious damage to all of medicine. So too they say that these same three principles are to be considered together with their conjoined qualities.

units.la: C cipia tria cū qualitatibus coniugatis çonsideranda esse dicunt. Verbi gratia: Sal cum qualitatibus coniugatis, aut est calidior & siccior: aut calidior & humidior: aut frigidior & humidior: aut frigidior & siccior. Sic etiam Sulphur, aut est calidius & siccius, aut calidius & humidius: aut frigidius & siccius: aut frigidius & humidius. Sic denique Mercurius, aut est calidior & siccior: aut calidior & humidior: aut frigidior & siccior: aut frigidior & humidior. Quod si συζυγίαι istæ principiorum trium cum qualitatibus illis extra naturam & temperamentū excedentibus, morborum causas ὁμογόνως constituunt, fieri non posse, ut vllo tempore morbos illos, quorū sunt causæ ὁμόγονοι, incomitatos relinquant. Verbi gratia: quoties sal exi-stit calidior, morbus iste existit. Quum erit Sal calidior, morbus iste erit. Quum extitit sal calidior, morbus iste extitit. Sic etiam causas ὁμογόνως Febrium, exempli causa, ponunt. Cum enim febris essentia sit calor præter naturam: non solum qualiqualitatem aliquā & accidens, quod sit antecedens attributi: verum etiam naturam quandā quæ sit consequens subiecti, ad constituendum medium demonstrationis, adhibendam esse aiunt. Porrò, aut salem: aut sulphur: aut certè spiritum illum vagum, hoc est, tenuissimam & maximè dissipabilem illam sulphuris siue olei portionem, quæ in arteriis & in corde existit, esse consequens illud μέλιςα καθόλε, quod ad constituēdas febriū causas ὁμοιογνὰς sit necessarium. Sic igitur in febribus, quæ sunt morbi similares, causas ὁμοιογνὰς perquirunt.
units.tr: For example: Salt, with its conjoined qualities, is either hotter and drier, or hotter and moister, or colder and moister, or colder and drier. So too Sulphur, is either hotter and drier, or hotter and moister, or colder and drier, or colder and moister. Finally, likewise Mercury, is either hotter and drier, or hotter and moister, or colder and drier, or colder and moister. But if these conjugations [συζυγίαι] of the three principles with those qualities exceeding nature and temperament constitute the causes of diseases homogonously, then it cannot happen that at any time they leave unaccompanied those diseases of which they are the homogonous causes. For example: whenever salt exists hotter, that disease exists. When salt will be hotter, that disease will be. When salt has been hotter, that disease has been. Likewise they posit homogonous causes of fevers, for example. For since the essence of fever is heat beyond nature, they say that one must bring in, to constitute the middle term of the demonstration, not only some quality and accident which is the antecedent of the attribute, but also some nature which is the consequent of the subject. Further, they say that either salt, or sulphur, or certainly that wandering spirit, that is, that most subtle and most dissipable portion of sulphur or oil which exists in the arteries and in the heart, is that consequent universal [μέλιςα καθόλε] which is necessary for constituting the homogonous causes of fevers. Thus, in fevers, which are similar diseases, they seek out the homogonous causes.

units.la: Quum Spiritus ille vagus, inquiunt, siue tenuissima illa substantia & portio sulphuris siue olei cordis, præter naturam incalescit, fit febris Ephemera. Si incalescet, fiet. Si iam incaluit, facta est febris Ephemera. Itē Quum salis liquor, hoc est sanguis, in venis præter naturam absque putredine incalescit, & calore isto cor affici incipit: fit Synochos febris non putrida. Si iam incaluit, & cor affectum est: facta est Synochos non putrida. Sin incalescet: fiet. Item: Quum salis liquor in venis non solum incalescit, veru-etiam putrescit, & putrem vaporem cum calore in cor fundere incipit: fit Synochos putrida, Si iam incaluit & putruit: facta est febris Synochos putrida. Sin incalescet: fiet. Item: quum ipsum cordis sulphur calidius euadit, adeo ut progressus fiat per primum & secundum Hecticae gradum: fit febris hectica. At quum calor ille immanis sulphur cordis primigenium inuasit. facta est febris hectica. Sin inuadet: fiet febris illa. Et quoniam praestantissimis medicis huius saeculi, de febribus intermittentibus compertum est, earum materiā nō è venis in corporis habitum propelli, neque esse venarum succum alendo corpori destinatum: sed esse materiam superuacaneam vel tartaream, ut quum Paracelso loquar, cuius sedes & origo sit in prima corporis regione, nempe circū ventriculū diaphragma, iecoris caua, lienem, pancreas, omentum, aut mesenteriū, & circum publicam illam corporis sentisentinam,quæ est in infero ventre:i-starum quoque febrium intermitten tium causas ὁμογόνως esse peruéstigan das. Sic igitur in istis quoq; febribus, causarum ὁμογόνων exempla ponunt. Quum calore immodico salis (cuius quidem salis vis in ventre infero est præcipua,vt dictum est) materia bilis superuacanea non solùm inceditur, verumetiā putrescit & vapor calórq; ad cor ascēdere incipiūt,fit febris ter tiana intermittens. Quod si materia illa superuacanea iam accensa est & putruit,facta est tertiana febris. Sin accendetur & putrescet:fiet tertiana febris. Item: materia melancholica, siue sit sex & limus,siue sit ex bile ex-usta aut ex humero alio exusto, quū putrescit & calore salis immodico accenditur, adeò vt vapor calórque ad cor contendere incipiant: fit quar tana intermittens. Si iam materia illa putruit & accensa est, & ad cor per-uenerunt vapor colórque : facta est quartana. Sin putrescet & accendetur,&ad cor peruenie̅t calor ille præ- ter naturam:febris quartana fiet.Cæ- terum, duplicem materiam à Para- celso poni: vnam tartarcam: alteram cruoris : atque vtramque materiam præter tria principia,& quatuor qua- litates,ab eodem Paracelso poni, in- fra demonstrabimus. Neque verò in morbis similaribus duntaxat causas illas ὁμοιομερὴς animaduertendas esse aiunt: verum etiam in morbis orga- nicis siue instrumentariis. Partes e- nim corporis esse subiecta dicũt,quæ ὁμοιομερῆ γένη ab Aristotele vocan- tur. Morbos esse attributa siue πάθη, quæ de subiectis dicuntur. At princi- pia illa esse consequentia partium. Qualitates verò intemperatas, siue ἀσυνπρασίας, esse antecedentia attribu- torum. Ex consequentibus illis, hoc est,ex principiis, & ex antecedenti- bus,id est,qualitatibus extra modum & naturam excedentibus in vnum conductis constare media Analyti- ca, siue causas ὁμοιομερὴς, quibus adhibitis morbi de partibus corporis demonstrantur. Exemplum causæ ὁμο-γόνῳ in morbis Organicis erit huiusmodi. Quum vis falis in renibus, aut in vesica coagulat materiam tartaream: (neque enim Paracelsistæ materiam prætermittunt, sed quemadmodum nos, interdum intemperie solitariam, interdum etiam intemperiem cum materia coniunctam consideramus: ita etiam isti principia illa tria calidiora, frigidiora, humidiora, siccior a, interdum sine materia: interdum cum materia cruoris aut tartari, ut infra dicemus, considerant.)
units.tr: When that vague spirit, they say, or that most subtle substance and portion of the sulphur or oil of the heart, grows hot contrary to nature, an ephemeral fever arises. If it will grow hot, it will arise. If it has already grown hot, an ephemeral fever has arisen. Likewise, when the liquor of salt, that is, the blood, grows hot in the veins contrary to nature, without putrefaction, and the heart begins to be affected by that heat: a synochus fever, not putrid, arises. If it has already grown hot and the heart has been affected: a synochus not putrid has arisen. If it will grow hot: it will arise. Likewise: when the liquor of salt in the veins not only grows hot but also putrefies, and begins to pour its putrid vapour with heat into the heart: a putrid synochus arises. If it has already grown hot and putrefied: a putrid synochus fever has arisen. If it will grow hot: it will arise. Likewise: when the sulphur of the heart itself becomes hotter, so that the progress is through the first and second degrees of hectic: a hectic fever arises. But when that monstrous heat has invaded the primary sulphur of the heart, a hectic fever has arisen. If it will invade: that fever will arise. And since it has been established by the most eminent physicians of this age, concerning intermittent fevers, that their matter is not driven from the veins into the habit of the body, nor is it the juice of the veins destined to nourish the body, but is a superfluous or tartarous matter, as I would speak with Paracelsus, whose seat and origin is in the first region of the body, namely around the stomach, the diaphragm, the hollow of the liver, the spleen, the pancreas, the omentum or mesentery, and around that common sink of the body which is in the lower belly: the causes of these intermittent fevers too must be investigated as homogeneous causes. So, in these fevers too, they set out examples of homogeneous causes. When the superfluous bile matter, through the immoderate heat of salt (whose power is chiefly in the lower belly, as has been said), not only catches fire but also putrefies, and its vapour and heat begin to ascend to the heart, a tertian intermittent fever arises. If that superfluous matter has already caught fire and putrefied, a tertian fever has arisen. If it will catch fire and putrefy, a tertian fever will arise. Likewise: melancholic matter, whether it be dregs and mud, or be from bile burnt up or from another burnt humour, when it putrefies and is set on fire by the immoderate heat of salt, so that vapour and heat begin to strive towards the heart: a quartan intermittent fever arises. If that matter has already putrefied and been set on fire, and the vapour and heat have reached the heart: a quartan has arisen. If it will putrefy and catch fire, and that heat contrary to nature will reach the heart: a quartan fever will arise. Moreover, that Paracelsus posits a double matter: one tartarean, the other of crude blood; and that he posits both matters, besides three principles and four qualities, we shall demonstrate below. Nor indeed, they say, are those homogeneous causes to be noted only in homogeneous diseases, but also in organic or instrumental diseases. For they say that the parts of the body are the subjects, which are called homogeneous kinds by Aristotle. The diseases are the attributes or affections, which are said of the subjects. But those principles are the consequences of the parts. The intemperate qualities, or dyscrasias, are the antecedents of the attributes. From those consequents, that is, from the principles, and from the antecedents, that is, the qualities exceeding the measure and nature, brought together into one, the middle terms of analysis, or homogeneous causes, are composed, by means of which diseases are demonstrated in relation to the parts of the body. An example of a homogeneous cause in organic diseases will be of this kind. When the power of salt in the kidneys or in the bladder coagulates the tartarean matter (for the Paracelsians do not neglect the matter, but, as we do, sometimes consider intemperance alone and sometimes intemperance joined with matter, so they too consider those three principles, warmer, colder, moister, drier, sometimes without matter, sometimes with the matter of crude blood or of tartar, as we shall say below).

units.la: Quum vis salis, inquiunt, in renibus, aut in vesica materiam coagulat, fit calculus. Quod si vis salis coagulauit, factus est calculus. Sin coagulabit, fiet calculus. Quod si quis obiiciat hoc modo calculum dici morbum: calculū autem esse substantiam: ac proinde morbum fore substantiam. Respondent materiam illam tartaream calculi esse causam materialem, quæ cum vi salis coagulante coniungenda est. Interdum enim pro morbo : interdum pro causa materiali:interdū pro causa obstruente, calculum vsurpari. Neq; esse substantiam,sed esse affectum praeter naturam, quum pro morbo vsurpatur.
units.tr: When the power of salt, they say, coagulates the matter in the kidneys, or in the bladder, a stone arises. If the power of salt has coagulated, a stone has arisen. If it will coagulate, a stone will arise. But if anyone objects that in this way a stone is called a disease, while a stone is a substance, and so a disease would be a substance: they reply that that tartarean matter is the material cause of the stone, which must be joined with the coagulating power of salt. For the word stone is sometimes used for the disease, sometimes for the material cause, sometimes for the obstructing cause. And it is not a substance, but an affection contrary to nature, when it is used for the disease.

units.la: Quod si quis, ob id quia calculus modo pro causa materiali , modo pro causa obstruente, modo pro morbo vsurpatur, inuolutum & obscurum exemplum esse queratur: afferunt aliud exemplum. Verbi gratia: aiunt fieri pleuritin veram, siue inflammationem eius membranae quae costis subtenditur : quum siue sal, siue liquor salis, siue sanguis, (dictum est enim principium & consequens summum iecoris esse salem, qui per venas in omnes corporis partes diducitur:)ex vena caua cordi assidente in eam quae azygos appellatur: ac dein in tenues costarum venas impetu quodam incurrit, ex quibus apertis aut disruptis exilit, incidítque aut in musculos mesopleurios,aut inter costas & stas & succingentem membranam, illícque collectus phlegmonem parit. Factam esse pleuritim, quum sal exiliit,incidítque,atque phlegmone peperit.Futuram pleuritim,si sal exiliet,incidétque,atque phlegmonem pariet.Excitari autem simul cū pleuritide vera febrem assiduā, quia propter vicinitate cordis, calor accesus in sale facile ad cor peruenit. Aliud etiā exemplū afferūt. Aiūt fieri ophtalmiam siue oculi phlegmonem, quum tenuis feruidúsq; sal in oculos fluit, è temporū angulorúmq; venis in obscuras & latetes oculorum venas irrues. Factā esse,quū fluxit: futurā esse,quū fluet. Sic in morbo cōmu ni,hoc est, in solutione cōtinuitatis, causæ ὁμοιόνῳ locū dari affirmat hūc in modū. Verbi gratia: quum diuiditur aut sal,aut sulphur,aut Mercuri⁹, in partibus similaribus aut organicis fit solutio continuitatis. Quod si iā diuisus est sal, aut Mercurius: aut si sulphur diuisum est in partibus similaribus aut organicis: hoc est, si partes illæ, aut ex sale, aut ex sulphure, aut ex Mercurio (ista enim tria sunt principia & consequentia, vt sæpe dictum est) aut certè ex his tribus conflatæ & compositæ, seorsim, aut simul omnes diuisæ sunt: tunc facta est solutio continuitatis. Sin partes illæ diuidentur, futurum vt sit solutio continuitatis. Quod si quis reperiatur, qui Δυσχεραίνῃ παυσλήνως, & fastidiosè repudiet vocabula ista, salis, sulphuris, Mercurij: respondent res ipsas, quas in natura positas esse constat, nondum alia nomina commodiora inuenisse, vt etiam paulò ante dictum est. Non posse aliter fumi consequentia partium corporis, in quibus morbi insunt, vt dictum est, quàm si tria ista principia ponantur, cum quatuor qualitatibus, quemadmodum etiam à Theodoro Duca ponütur in libris De communicatione naturali, propter prætermissionem trium istorum principiorum, quæ consequentia esse affirmant
units.tr: But if anyone complains that, because a stone is sometimes used for the material cause, sometimes for the obstructing cause, sometimes for the disease, the example is involved and obscure, they bring forward another example. For instance, they say that true pleurisy arises, or the inflammation of that membrane which is stretched under the ribs, when either salt, or a liquor of salt, or blood (for it has been said that the chief principle and consequent of the liver is salt, which is spread through the veins into all parts of the body) rushes with a certain force from the hollow vein, lying beside the heart, into the vein called azygos, and then into the thin veins of the ribs, from which, when they are opened or broken, it bursts out and falls either into the mesopleural muscles or between the ribs and the membrane that surrounds them, and there, gathered together, it produces a phlegmon. Pleurisy has arisen when the salt has burst out, fallen, and produced a phlegmon. Pleurisy will arise if the salt will burst out, fall, and produce a phlegmon. And a continual fever is said to be excited together with true pleurisy, because, owing to the nearness of the heart, the heat kindled in the salt easily reaches the heart. They bring forward another example too. They say that ophthalmia, or a phlegmon of the eye, arises when thin and fiery salt flows into the eyes, rushing from the veins of the temples and the corners into the hidden and secret veins of the eyes. It has arisen since it flowed; it will arise since it will flow. Thus in a common disease, that is, in a solution of continuity, they affirm that a place is given to homogeneous causes in this manner. For instance: when salt, or sulphur, or mercury is divided, a solution of continuity occurs in the similar or organic parts. If salt or mercury is already divided, or if sulphur has been divided in the similar or organic parts: that is, if those parts, made either of salt, or of sulphur, or of mercury (for these three are principles and consequents, as has often been said), or certainly composed and put together from these three, are divided separately or all together, then a solution of continuity has arisen. If those parts will be divided, a solution of continuity will come about. But if anyone is found who, with a sour and disdainful distaste, rejects these words, salt, sulphur, mercury: they reply that they have not yet found more convenient names for the things themselves, which are constantly found in nature, as was also said a little before. The consequents of the parts of the body, in which the diseases lie, cannot otherwise be grasped, as has been said, than if these three principles are posited together with the four qualities, just as they are also posited by Theodorus Duca in his books On natural communication, on account of the omission of those three principles, which they affirm to be consequents.

units.la: firmant & κατὰ πάντος, id est, de constitutione omnis corporis & partiū eius, Galeni sectatores, è quorum numero nos esse profitemur, non posse commodè & diserte causas ὁμογόνους afferre, neque illas posse à morbis distinguere. Verbi gratia: confundunt causam ὁμόγονον cum morbo, quoties dicunt hunc vel illum morbum esse intemperie, aut calidam, aut frigidam, aut humidam, aut siccam: istud autem vsu venire nobis, quia consequentia illa tria nondum nobis perspecta sunt.
units.tr: affirm also, and κατὰ πάντος, that is, concerning the constitution of every body and of its parts, the followers of Galen, of whose number we profess ourselves to be, that they cannot conveniently and clearly bring forward homogeneous causes, nor can they distinguish them from diseases. For instance, they confuse the homogeneous cause with the disease whenever they say that this or that disease is an intemperature, either hot, or cold, or moist, or dry: and this happens to us, they say, because those three consequents are not yet clearly known to us.

units.la: Atqui dicendum fuit, inquiunt, Verbi gratia: aut salem, aut Mercurium calidiorem, aut sulphur calidius esse causam ὁμόγονον morbi illius calidi, siue intemperiei illius calidae. Quinetiam trium capacitatum, videlicet, capitis, thoracis, vētris inferi, vnamquamque suo principi viscerl, atque adeo suo consequenti, & quasi principio proprio assignandam fuisse aiunt, vt etiam infra dicemus.
units.tr: But, they say, it should have been stated like this, for example: either salt, or a hotter Mercury, or a hotter sulphur is the homogonous cause [ὁμόγονον] of that hot disease, or of that hot intemperie. Moreover, they say that each of the three cavities, namely of the head, chest, and lower belly, should be assigned to its own principal viscus, and so to its own consequent and, as it were, proper principle, as we shall also say below.

units.la: Sicut enim iecori ex tribus principibus visceribus vni, inferus venter assignatur:ita etiam eandem capacitatē sali assignandam fuisse, tanquam iecoris consequenti & principio.Item: sicut cordi principi visceri media capacitas assignatur : ita etiam eandem capacitatem oleo siue sulphuri assignā dam fuisse,tanquam consequēti cordis & principio. Quemadmodum e-nim tenuis & sincerus aër (inquit Fer-nelius)iccirco est necessarius,vt flam-mæ tanquam pabulum accedat, & libero flatu alius aliúsque accedens, quasi pastionem se offerat flammæ deuorandam : ita etiam in media capacitate, nēpe in thorace, à pulmone spiritum identidem reciprocādo duci reddíque (inquit; idem Fernelius)atque haustum hunc cōfici præpararíque cordi:cuius demum accessu innatus calor ventilatus refrigeretur,& vitalis spiritus alatur foueatúrque tanquam pabulo. units.tr: For just as the lower belly is assigned to the liver, one of the three principal viscera, so the same cavity should also be assigned to salt, as the consequent and principle of the liver. Likewise, just as the middle cavity is assigned to the heart, the principal viscus, so the same cavity should also be assigned to oil or sulphur, as the consequent and principle of the heart. For just as thin and pure air (says Fernel) is necessary so that the flame may receive it as fuel, and as, with free breathing, one portion of air after another comes forward and offers itself as food for the flame to devour, so too in the middle cavity, namely the chest, the breath is drawn in and expelled again and again from the lungs (says Fernel again), and this inhalation is made and prepared for the heart. By its approach the innate heat is cooled by ventilation, and the vital spirit is nourished and cherished as if by fuel. Finally, just as the citadel, that is the head, is assigned to the brain, the principal viscus and the animal spirit itself, so the same cavity should be assigned to Mercury, as consequent and principle.

Et, quemadmodum primò tres quasi bullæ, sunt rudimenta trium illorum præstantissimorum viscerum, & quasi primordia omnium corporis partium: ita etiam trium rudimentorum sive primordiorum, tria ista, salem, sulphur, Mercurium, esse consequentia & principia. Seminis portiones (inquit Fernelius) quæ à tribus parentum principiis defluxerunt, comparent imprimis medio femine in tres quasi bullas digestas, spiritu facultateque confertas. Eæ rudimenta sunt iecoris, cordis, & cerebri.
