units.tr: Physiology, book 4, chapter 3: the same cavity should be assigned to Mercury, as consequent and principle. And just as, at first, three small bubbles are the rudiments of those three most excellent viscera, and as it were the beginnings of all the parts of the body, so too these three rudiments or beginnings, salt, sulphur and Mercury, are consequent and principles. The portions of the seed (says Fernel) that have flowed down from the three principles of the parents first appear in the middle of the seed as three bubbles, as it were, arranged and endowed with spirit and faculty. These are the rudiments of the liver, heart and brain. So in Hippocrates, in the book Περὶ ἀρχῶν (for it should read περὶ ἀρχῶν, not περὶ σαρκῶν), the nature and condition of salt are attributed to the liver: "Thus the liver is composed" (says Hippocrates), "for when, out of the warm flesh, what was left over among the abundant and fatty parts was compacted, the cold overcame the warm and it congealed" [ὥδε δὲ ξυνέστηκε τὸ ἧπαρ, ξυνοῦ τῆς θερμῆς σαρκὸς ἀπολειφθὲν ἀνὰ τὸ πολλῶδες καὶ τὸ λιπαρόν, ἐκράτησε τὸ ψυχρὸν τοῦ θερμοῦ, ἢ ἐπάγη]. That is: "But the liver is compacted in this way. When, along with the warm, much moisture was enclosed without any glutinous or fatty part, the cold overcame the warm and it congealed."

units.la: Fernel. lib. phys. 7. cap. 10. multum humidi coclusum esset absque glutinoso & pingui, calidum à frigido superatum est & congelatū. Quod si quis dicat, sanguinem frigore, salem contra igni coagulari: Respondent, sanguinem quoque posse igni frigi, ita ut aqueus humor exhaletur, quemadmodum fit in sale. Addunt praeterea reperiri salem, qui igni liquetur, & frigidi aëris occursu cogatur. Sic sal petrae, quem vocant, & nitrum igni liquantur, & frigore coguntur. Quod ad cor attinet: cordi naturam & conditionem olei siue sulphuris tribui eodem in libro, his verbis. Τὸ Θερμὸν, inquit, τῆς λιπαρᾶς μητρόπολις. id est. Calidum est sedes & metropolis eius quod pingue est. Et paulò post: τὸ Θερμὸν, inquit, ὡλεῖσον ἐν τῆσι φλεψὶν ἡ τῇ καρδίᾳ. ἡ διὰ τοῦτο ὠνευμαν καρδίᾳ ἔχει Θερμὴν ἐσσα μάλιστα τῷ ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ. Ἐστι δὲ ἡ ἄλλως γνῶναι. Πῦρ εἴτις Θέλει καίειν ἐν οἰκήματι, ὁπόταν ἄνεμος μὴ εἰσπνέῃ φλόξ κινεῖται, τότε μὲν μάλλον, τότε ὁ ἡ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸν αὐτὸν τὸν τρόπον κινέεται.&c.id est.Calidum plurimum in arteriis, & in corde inest. Ob id cor habet spiritum, nepe quia est calidissimum eorum omniū quæ in homine insunt.Hoc ipsum licet etiam alio modo intelligere. Siquis ignem in ædibus accendat, etiamsi flamma nullius venti flatu agitetur, tamen mouetur,interdum magis,interdum minus. Sic etiam lucerna accensa eodem modo mouetur. Et paulò post. Τεχμήρια ἡ τουτέων. Εἴτις ἐθέλοι ὁπίσαν νόυρωπέα τε καὶ κολλώδεα, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἡ. Τὰ μὲν ἄλλα ταχὺ ὁπίσατα: τὰ ἡ νόυρωπέα καὶ κολλώδεα ἂν ἐθέλει ὁπιλάδς. Ἐλάχιστον γὰρ ἔχει τὸ λιπαρές. Τὸ ἡ ᾧ ιότατον καὶ λιπαςὲν τάχιςα ὁπίατα. id est: Horum signa atque argumenta sunt ista. Si quis neruosa & glutinosa assare conetur, quum cætera facile citóque assentur, neruosa certè & glutinosa assari nequeunt. Nam minimum habent eius quod pinguè est. Id autem quod pinguissimum est, celerrimè assatur. Hęc Hippocrates in libro περὶ ἀρχῶν. Reuertor ad indicationes. Aiunt Paracelsi sectatores, morbum eum, quem nos organicum vocamus, æquè esse communem morbum atque est solutio continuitatis. Omnes enim corporis partes pendere ex tribus illis principibus viscerib⁹, iecore, corde, cerebro: cúmq; tria illa viscera, statim in principio, ante reliquas corporis partes, habeant sua rudimenta, non posse fieri, quin sal, sulphur, Mercurius (quip(quippe quæ sunt consequentia, & principia trium illorum præstantissimorum viscerum) sint etiam principia & consequentia omnium corporis partium, quæcunque illæ sint, hoc est, siue sint similares, siue organicæ. Consequentia enim, (vt diximus in Tractatu eo qui est De innestigandis principiis syllogismorum omnium,) appellari illa, quæ latissimè omnium pateant. Tria ista, salem, sulphur, Mercurium in omnibus comperiri:in ipsis etiam remediis: quæ quidem remedia ex maiore mundo in minorem, nempe in hominem comportanda sunt:ac propterea tria ista,salem,sulphur,& Mercurium,esse consequentia & principia, tum corporis humani, tum etiam remediorum omnium. Sic enim constare nobis συμπάθειαν omnium rerum, & geminam illam Anatomen, de qua supra dictum est: siquidem sal externus,sali interno:& sulphur externū, sulphuri interno:& Mercurius externus, Mercurio interno συμπάσχει. Quod si ἀντιπάσχοντα requiris: reperietur sal externus, qui sali interno: reperietur sulphur externum, quod sulphuri interno: denique reperietur Mercurius externus, qui interno ἀντιπάσχῃ. Proinde Anatomas istorum trium, salis, sulphuris, Mercurij, quæ sunt consequentia triū illorum principum viscerum, diligenter obseruandas esse in maiore mundo, vt quoties requirit Microcosmus, adhibeantur. Quod ad salem attinet: affirmant docti viri etiam præter Paracelsitas, milites vulneratos solo salis pugno alligato cauere, ne putredo, aut inflammatio, aut sphacelus, vel gangræna suboriantur. Ergo sal, inquiunt, qui est proprius iecoris & venarum, indicat salem remedium.
units.tr: Fernel, Physiology, book 7, chapter 10. If anyone says that blood is coagulated by cold but salt by fire, they reply that blood too can be frozen by fire, so that the watery humour is exhaled, just as happens with salt. They add that there is also a salt that melts in fire and is solidified by the approach of cold air. Thus rock salt, as it is called, and nitre melt in fire and are congealed by cold. As for the heart, in the same book the nature and condition of oil or sulphur are attributed to it, in these words: "The warm is the seat and metropolis of what is fatty" [τὸ θερμὸν τῆς λιπαρῆς μητρόπολις]. And a little later: "The warm is found most of all in the arteries and in the heart. For this reason the heart has spirit, being the hottest of all the things that are in the human being" [τὸ θερμὸν μάλιστα ἐν τῇσι φλεψὶν ἔνι καὶ ἐν τῇ καρδίῃ. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡ καρδίη πνεῦμα ἔχει, θερμωτάτη ἐοῦσα μάλιστα τῶν ἐν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ]. "This may also be understood in another way: if someone sets fire to a fire in a house, even though the flame is not moved by any wind's blast, it still moves, sometimes more, sometimes less. So too a lit lamp moves in the same way." Finally, in the same book the nature and condition of Mercury are attributed to the brain, in these words: "The brain is the seat and metropolis of what is cold and glutinous" [ὁ ἐγκέφαλος ἐστι μητρόπολις τῆς ψυχρῆς ἢ τῆς κολλώδεος]. And a little later: "For this reason the brain, because it has very little of what is fatty and most of what is glutinous, cannot be burnt by the heat" [διὰ τοῦτο ὁ ἐγκέφαλος, ὅτι ὀλίγιστον ἔχει τῆς λιπαρῆς, τῆς δὲ πολλώδεος πλεῖστον, οὐ δύναται ἐκκαυθῆναι ἀπὸ τῆς θερμῆς]. And a little later: "The signs and proofs of these things are these. If anyone should try to roast sinewy and glutinous things and the others, the others are quickly roasted, but the sinewy and glutinous cannot be roasted. For they have very little of what is fatty. What is very scant and very fatty is roasted most quickly" [τεκμήρια δὲ τούτων· εἴ τις ἐθέλοι ὀπτᾶν νευρώδεα καὶ κολλώδεα, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἡδέα. τὰ μὲν ἄλλα ταχὺ ὀπτᾶται· τὰ δὲ νευρώδεα καὶ κολλώδεα οὐ δύναται ὀπτᾶσθαι. Ἐλάχιστον γὰρ ἔχει τὸ λιπαρές. τὸ δὲ ὀλιγιστότατον καὶ λιπαρώτατον τάχιστα ὀπτᾶται]. Thus far Hippocrates in the book Περὶ ἀρχῶν. I return to the indications. The followers of Paracelsus say that the disease which we call organic is as common as a solution of continuity. For all the parts of the body depend on those three principal viscera, the liver, heart and brain; and since those three viscera have their rudiments at the very beginning, before the other parts of the body, it cannot be that salt, sulphur and Mercury (being the consequents and principles of those three most excellent viscera) are not also the principles and consequents of all the parts of the body, whatever they are, that is, whether they are similar or organic. For consequents (as we said in the treatise On Investigating the Principles of All Syllogisms) are those things that extend most widely of all. These three, salt, sulphur and Mercury, are found in all things, and even in the remedies themselves; and these remedies must be brought from the greater world into the lesser, that is, into the human being. Therefore these three, salt, sulphur and Mercury, are the consequents and principles both of the human body and of all remedies. For in this way the sympathy [συμπάθεια] of all things is established for us, and that twofold anatomy of which we spoke above: since the external salt sympathizes [συμπάσχει] with the internal salt, the external sulphur with the internal sulphur, and the external Mercury with the internal Mercury. But if you ask for the antipathy [ἀντιπάσχοντα]: there will be found an external salt which acts against the internal salt, there will be found an external sulphur which acts against the internal sulphur, and finally there will be found an external Mercury which acts against the internal Mercury. Therefore the anatomies of these three, salt, sulphur and Mercury, which are the consequents of those three principal viscera, are to be carefully observed in the greater world, so that they may be applied whenever the microcosm requires. As for salt, learned men, even apart from the Paracelsians, affirm that soldiers who are wounded are protected, by salt alone bound on the wound, from putrefaction, inflammation, sphacelus or gangrene arising. Therefore salt, they say, which is proper to the liver and veins, indicates salt as the remedy.

units.la: Sic sulphur siue oleum, quod est proprium cordis & Arteriarum, indicat sulphur siue oleum. Nam olei naturâ aërea cor recreatur atq; reficitur: & olei, pabulíque eiusmodi aërei beneficio neficio Marasmus à corde auertitur.
units.tr: So too sulphur or oil, which is proper to the heart and arteries, indicates sulphur or oil. For the airy nature of oil refreshes and restores the heart, and by the help of oil and of such airy nourishment, wasting is turned away from the heart.

units.la: Τρέφεται, inquit Hippocrates, ὅτε σιτί-οισιν, ὅτε ποτοῖσιν ἀπὸ τῆς γνδύος. ἀλλὰ καὶ θαρῇ ἢ φωτοειδὲι ἐωξεσίη γεγονυῖη ἐκ τῆς διαπρίσιος τῆς αἵματος. id est: cor alitur, nō efculentis, non poculentis proximè à vētre acceptis:fed pura & lumi nofa fubftantia, quæ ex difcretione fanguinis exiftit. Sic denique Mercu rius fiue liquor ille præftantiffimus, fiue vapor ignem fugiēs, qui cerebri & neruorum proprius eft, vt fæpe di-ctum eft,indicat Mercurium fiue na-turam Mercurialem. Sed infra e-tiam quum rationem vtendi exponemus, de his ad Paracelfi doctrinam accommodatè dicemus. Ex iis quæ adhuc dicta funt & commemorata, intelligimus tria ista principia, falē, fulphur, & Mercurium, ex obferuationibus rerum metallicarum, & operationibus Alchimiæ in scientiā medendi Paracelsum transtulisse. Sed Paracelsi sectatores, dum negligunt intemperies illas, calidum, frigidam,humidam,siccam,& totidem co- iugatas nempe:calidam & siccam: calidam & humidam:frigidam & siccam: frigidam & humidam:temerè, nulla habi ta ratione τῆς ἐμπυρόυματος, remedia exhibent: neque sine periculo, præ- sertim quum sumuntur ad morbos interiores: siquidem remedia etiam absque præparatione illa chemica cōmodè & vtiliter vsurpari possunt. Galeni verò sectatores, dum omnia metiuntur qualitatibus & temperamentis,incurrunt in errores grauissimos.Sapore multa aut profutura,aut nihil certè nocitura putantur, inquit Ferneli, quæ sæpe vidi tacitis viribus, sola obseruatione noscendis, alia sumta,alia solùm admota, in perniciem summam,& exitium miseros præcipitare.Hæc Fernelius,quç etiam supra à nobis citata sunt. Ex his etiam intelligimus,quanti faciēda sit Anatome illa magna viuáque, per quam non solùm qualitates & temperamenta: non solùm principia illa Paracelsica: verumetiam, ipsam remedii medii formam & entelechiam ex fi-gnis ὅτι ἐςὶ, cognoscimus.Sed ante-quam ad utendi modum veniam, de materia,quę interdum coniuncta est cum intemperie,dicendum est.Om-nis enim intemperies,aut est solitaria: aut est coniuncta cum materia. Paracel-so materia vna est cruoris: altera tartarea: tertia, mixta ex materia cruoris, & materia tartarea. Materia cruoris ab interioribus illis principiis proficiscitur,nempe à sale, sulphure, Mercurio partium, ex quibus constat corpus humanum.Differt à materia tartarea, eo quod materia tartarea fit illa,quæ ab esculentis & poculentis profecta in ventriculo concoqui non potuit. Materia autem cruoris à principiis illis interioribus, ex quibus constat corpus humanum, proficiscatur. Iccirco in libro priore De vrinis,monet Paracelsus,si vrinam cruoris colligere voluerus,ut nihil comedas, nec bibas:aut saltem siccum panem,aut siccam carnem, ut est assata: & tunc colligatur ea vrina, quæ post mediam noctem venit. Quod si contingeret, ut ægrotus laboraret aliquo morbo acuto, inquit Paracelsus, qui nihil quidè comedit, sed interim largiter bibit, is admonendus est, ut unica saltem nocte nihil biberat, quò vrina certa cruoris colligi posset: Aliàs enim falsum vrinæ indicium redderetur. Nam licet & à cibo & à potu abstineas, tamen natura cotidie per seipsam dat suum cruorem. Ea enim quæ sunt in natura mineralia, nempe sal, sulphur, & Mercurius, cotidie mittunt hunc cruorem. Hæc Paracelsus de cruore siue de humore ab illis tribus principiis interioribus profecto.
units.tr: "The heart is nourished," says Hippocrates, "not by solid foods nor by drinks received directly from the stomach, but by a pure and luminous substance which arises from the separation of the blood" [τρέφεται, φησὶν Ἱπποκράτης, οὐ σιτίοισιν, οὐ ποτοῖσιν ἀπὸ τῆς γαστρὸς, ἀλλὰ καθαρὴ καὶ φωτοειδὴς οὐσία γεγονυῖα ἐκ τῆς διακρίσιος τοῦ αἵματος]. So, finally, Mercury, or that most excellent liquid, or vapour fleeing from fire, which is proper to the brain and nerves, as has often been said, indicates Mercury or the Mercurial nature. But below, when we set out the manner of using remedies, we shall speak of these things in a way suited to the teaching of Paracelsus. From what has been said and recalled so far, we understand that these three principles, salt, sulphur and Mercury, Paracelsus transferred into the science of healing from observations of metallic things and the operations of alchemy. But the followers of Paracelsus, while they neglect those intemperies, hot, cold, moist, dry, and the combined ones, namely hot and dry, hot and moist, cold and dry, cold and moist, rashly administer remedies with no regard for their burning nature; and not without danger, especially when they are taken for internal diseases, since remedies can be used conveniently and usefully even without that chemical preparation. But the followers of Galen, while they measure everything by qualities and temperaments, fall into very grave errors. Many things are thought either to be useful or certainly not to harm by taste, says Fernel, which I have often seen, by their hidden powers, known only by observation, some taken, others merely applied, hurl wretched people into the greatest ruin and destruction. Thus Fernel, whom we have also cited above. From these things too we understand how much that great and living anatomy is to be valued, through which we know not only the qualities and temperaments, not only those Paracelsian principles, but also the very form and entelechy of the remedy itself, from the signs of that it is. But before I come to the manner of using, something must be said about matter, which is sometimes joined with intemperie. For every intemperie is either solitary or joined with matter. According to Paracelsus there is one matter of blood, another tartarean, and a third mixed from the matter of blood and the matter of tartar. The matter of blood proceeds from those inner principles, namely from the salt, sulphur and Mercury of the parts of which the human body is made. It differs from the tartarean matter in that the tartarean matter is that which, proceeding from food and drink, could not be digested in the stomach, whereas the matter of blood proceeds from those inner principles of which the human body consists. Therefore in the first book On Urines, Paracelsus advises: if you wish to collect urine of the blood, eat nothing and drink nothing, or at least dry bread or dried meat, such as roast meat; and then that urine is collected which comes after midnight. But if it should happen that the patient is suffering from some acute disease, says Paracelsus, and eats nothing indeed but drinks abundantly in the meantime, he is to be warned to drink nothing for at least one night, so that a certain urine of blood may be collected; otherwise a false sign from the urine would be produced. For although you abstain both from food and from drink, nature still gives its own blood each day by itself. For those things which are mineral in nature, namely salt, sulphur and Mercury, send out this blood every day. Thus Paracelsus concerning blood, or humour, which certainly comes from those three inner principles.

units.la: Materia tartarea illa est, inquit idè Paracelsus, quæ profecta ab alimentis, nempe ab esculentis & poculentis, non coquitur in ventriculo, neque in iecore, aut in venis mutatur in sanguinem, sed cùm sit mucilaginosa & quasi lutea coagulatur per Spiritum salis, in calculum aut arenulas. Nam, ut idem Paracelsus docet lib.1. De morbis tartareis cap. 5. Si materia tartarea & lutea in loca perueniat, in quibus non possit
units.tr: Tartareous matter is that, says Paracelsus in the same place, which, arising from food and drink, that is from edibles and potables, is not cooked in the stomach, nor in the liver, nor changed into blood in the veins, but, since it is mucilaginous and almost clayey, is coagulated by the spirit of salt into a stone or gravel. For, as the same Paracelsus teaches in book 1 On Tartareous Diseases, chapter 5: If tartareous and clayey matter reaches places in which it cannot

units.la: Paracels. lib. 2. de morbis tartareis in explicatione cap.1. possit coagulari: Verbi gratia: Si perueniat ad collum & ibi hæreat fiunt strumæ: quia videlicet materia illa destituitur à calore et spiritu salis coagulante. Hæc Paracelsus de materia tartarea. Cæterùm materia expurganda est, vt ipse Paracelsus docet in tractatibus De modo pharmacandi. Expurgandam esse, nobis cum Paracelso conuenit. Sed quidnam indicabit instrumentum siue medicamentum, quo adhibito siue exhibito purgare licebit? Vtrum materia ipsa purganda? An medicamentum externum purgans? Respondet Paracelsus, considerandos esse colores, qui sunt similes tum in materia expurganda, tum etiam in medicamento purgante. Verba Paracelsi hæc sunt. Colores, inquit, indicant morbos: quos hoc loco non describo: sed solùm indico, vt ster corum colores melius intelligantur. Qua de causa, quum tot colores perfecti sint in homine, quot in exteriore sphæra: sciendum est illud quod prædiximus de emunctoriis & virtutibus digestiuis, in illis esse multos ac diuersos colores, quos colores, stercus etiam extrinsecè retinet.Item paulò post.Colo-res, inquit,ostendunt morbos corporis, non stercoris.Stercus enim nihil est, nec sanita-tem,nec morbos efficit.Iccirco studere primò colorum habere cognitionem iuxta localem Anatomiam, quò sciatis ex colorum origi-ne,locorum colores,& per eos materiā mor-borum. Sic enim cognoscendi sunt colores, & genera stercorum:non vt stercora curen-tur medicina, sed loca ipsa vnde prodeunt.
units.tr: Paracelsus, book 2 On Tartareous Diseases, in the explanation of chapter 1: cannot be coagulated. For example: if it reaches the neck and sticks there, scrofulous swellings arise, because that matter is evidently deprived of the heat and the coagulating spirit of salt. So far Paracelsus on tartareous matter. Moreover, the matter must be purged, as Paracelsus himself teaches in his treatises On the Method of Pharmacy. We agree with Paracelsus that it must be purged. But what will indicate the instrument or medicine by which one may purge, when it is applied or administered? Is the matter itself to be purged, or an external purging medicine? Paracelsus answers that the colours must be considered, which are alike both in the matter to be purged and in the purging medicine. Paracelsus's words are these: Colours, he says, indicate diseases, which I do not describe in this place, but only point out, so that their kinds may be better understood. For this reason, since as many perfect colours exist in man as in the outer sphere, it must be understood that what we have said before about the excretory organs and the digestive powers, there are many and diverse colours in those, which colours the excrement also retains outwardly. Likewise a little later: Colours, he says, show the diseases of the body, not of the excrement. For excrement is nothing, and produces neither health nor disease. Therefore first study to have knowledge of the colours according to local anatomy, so that you may know from the origin of the colours the colours of the places, and through them the matter of the diseases. For in this way the colours and kinds of excrement are to be known, not so that the excrements may be cured by medicine, but the very places from which they come.

units.la: Hæc Paracelsus de inuestigādis me-dicamentis purgantibus. Quæ cùm ita sint, perspicuū est, indicationes ac-curatissimas ex Anatome illa magna petēdas esse,siue sit medendum mor-bis, siue sit purgandum.Sic calor cassiæ fistularis:forma fistulæ:grana ipsa digesta in fistula, indicant, ad quam materiam expurgandā cōparata sit. Sic Rheum-barbarum habet signa indicātia signis materiæ expurgandæ ἀντίσποφα. De-nique nullus est morbus siue sit simi-laris,siue sit organicus,siue sit solutio continui: id est morbus communis: siue morbus similaris sit solitarius, siue sit cum materia, modò morbus ille sit sanabilis: (nam claudos, verbi gratia, & cæcos persanare solius Dei est) Nullus inquâ, morbʾ est qui nō habeat sui remedii indicationé in Anatome illa magna. Sic vulnus recès factū, quod est solutio cōtinui, habet signū ἀντίσπροφον in Androsæmo: cuiˀ coma trita sanguineo succo manat, vt docet Plinius lib. 27. cap. 4. & Dioscorides lib.3.cap.146,& 148.Hyperici flos, inquit Dioscorides, digitis tritus sanguineum succum remittit, qua ex causa androsæmon cognominatur. Et in extremo capite 148.Vulneribus,inquit Dioscorides,sanguinem cohibet. Iccirco de ignoratione huius præstantissimæ Anatomes à Paracelso reprehendun tur medici vulgares, his verbis. Quoties nostri medici ægrotum curant, inquit, totum negotium versatur in fortuna. Fundamentum istorum est, Ensem efficere vulnus. Præter istud nihil sciunt. Gladius sanè non requirit medicinam: sed id quod ipsam postulat, est natura, quam igneram: solum vero gladium noverunt. Idem Paracelsus ad Anatomen magnam, cum locis prope infinitis, tum in extremo tractatu quarto De modo pharmacandi, exhortatur omnes diversis verbis Hominis parentes, inquit: sunt cælum & terra. Propterea etiam natus est ac creuit in ipsorum natura & partibus excepta imagine Dei. Sic nulla fit hic sparatio, nisi imaginis Dei. Natura permanet inseparabilis a patre & matre. Quum ergo parentes hominis sint cælum & terra ex quibus postremo creatus est discatus ex parentibus infantem: & Anatomiam exercete in parentibus. Eos dissecate, non pueros. ubi cælum & terram cognoveritis habebitis totius naturæ humanæ plenam scientiam. Hæc ille: quibus verbis monet omnes medicos, ut indicationes remediorum petat ex illa Anatome. Rationem addit: quia Entelechiæ & formæ omnes remediorum externorum propter hominem conditæ sunt & ad hominem referuntur: neque separari possunt a materia,id est à terra,ex qua procrea tæ sunt res illæ, non secus atque homo ipse.Nam Deus finxit ex terra ho minem. Iccirco formæ illæ non sunt χωριστοὶ, id est, non sunt separabiles à materia, siue in minore, siue in maiore mundo considerentur. At sola hominis anima est χωριστὸς, id est separabilis à materia:quia à flatu Dei in facie hominis inspirato proximè profecta est: vt diximus in orationibus Apodicticis De separabili natura animæ humanæ : & De resurrectione mortuorum. His ita declaratis venio ad vtendi rationem.In hac vtendi ratione,loca, per quæ materia expurgâda est, aut medicamentum sumendum:partem, cui adhibenda sunt remedia: Itémque tempus morbi & horam,quibus remedia vsurpanda sunt, consīderare oportet.Hoc in loco de locis, per quæ materia expurganda est,aut medicamentum sumendum : itémque de forma medicamentorum, quæ omnis aut liquida, aut solida est Fernelio, pauca dicemus. Tres sunt capacitates in templo corporis humani, ipsæ inter se distinctæ & locis disclusæ, quas etiam supra strictim & breuiter attigimus. inferus venter, siue infima capacitas est subter Diaphragma, siue subter septū transuersum, in qua sunt ventriculus, iecur, à quo venæ sursum deorsumq; diducuntur: in qua etiam sunt lien, renes, vesica, vterus. Media capacitas est thoracis, in qua sunt pulmones, & cor à quo Arteriæ. Summa capacitas est illa, quæ tanquam sacrarium summum, & quasi oraculorum locum constituit, quam quidem capacitatem caput appellamus. in qua sunt cerebrum, & membrana utraque: unde etiam neruorum septem coiugationes. In hac etiam est cerebellum, quod in spinæ medullam deriuatur, unde cæteri nerui prodeunt. Iam formas remediorum ad tres illas capacitates accommodemus. Sales, infimæ capacitati, quæ subter diaphragma est, conueniunt, vt dictum est. Ac salis quidem, vt & panis,& nis,&ciborū mansorū atq; mollitorū forma solida:Itémque forma liquida, œ-sophago, ventriculo: ac deinde iecori & lieni conuenire videtur. Sic Clysma-tum quoque forma liquida intesti-nis conuenit. Quod ad sales attinet: sal sali opponendus videtur. Verbi gratia:sali resoluto iecoris in hydro-pe opponendus est sal expellens sa-lem resolutum. Deinde exhibendus est sal corroborās. Sic in obstructio-nibus tum iecoris, tum lienis, exhi-bendi sunt sales eiusmodi, qui expe-diant obstructiones. Et quoniam ie-cori, quod est παρέγχυμα,siue Viscus sanguinis efficiens, sales conuenire videntur: etiam venis, quæ à iecore proficiscuntur, & partibus corporis, quâ sanguine aluntur,sales conuenire videbuntur. Hinc etiam sal vulne ribus recentibus accōmodatissimus, vt & saccharum. At verò mediæ capa-citati,quæ est Thoracis,magis conue nire videtur natura & forma eorum, quæ ignem concipiunt, nempe natura, sulphuris, olei, arteriacorum, vt tra-gachantæ, & aliorum eiusmodi. Pri-mum, media capacitas : qua parte summæ illi capitis capacitati proxi-ma est, propter pulmones, suffimen-tis iuuatur. Porrò sal ad suffimenta non est accommodatus, sed sulphur, vt etiam docet Dioscorides, lib.5.ca-pite 73. Prodest sulphur, inquit Diosco-rides, tussibus, suspiriosis, purulenta extus-sientibus in uno sumtu aut suffitum. Quod autem saccharum, & alij etiam sales, accommodatè ex Anatome selecti, vtiliter cū oleo, verbi gratia, amyg-dalino recenti, & arteriacis miscen-tur, id fit propter communicatione naturæ salis per venam cauam, quæ è iecoris connexo per diaphragma sursum fertur. Deinde, oleum, butyrum, quæ etiam non secus atque sulphur & capura siue camphora flammam concipiūt, arteriacis sunt similia. Ipsa quoque olea prudenter selecta ad illinen-dum pectus, Itémque ad tuendā protegendámque vnctură regione cor-dis, dis, sunt accommodatissima. Quinetiam luminari illi magno, nepe cordi, quod est tanquam sol in minore mundo. Si oleum suum non instilletur, non est dubium, quin vitalis ille calor extinguatur. Praeterea oleum etiam simplex sumtum, ut & butyrum: itemque suffimenta ex oleis & unguentis ido neis, ab arce vitae venena arcet. Observandum est autem diversa esse oleorum genera, quorum vires vsumque distincte nosse operae pretium est: sive expressa sint e fructibus, seminibus, & nucleis: sive e sale artificiose extracta sint. Summa capacitati, quae est capitis, conuenire videtur natura illa sive substantia Mercurialis, quae tum sale, tum oleo sive sulphure multo perfectior multoque elaboratior est. Nam spiritus animalis, qui est in cerebro, quique per neruorum ductus, tum in sensuum instrumenta, tum in Musculos motores profluit, ex vitali spiritu per ceruicis arterias in contextum admirabilem sublato, primum elaboratur, inquit Fernelius, deinde in interiore altero cerebri contextu, qui à secun dis nomen habet, vi cerebri ingenita, in ani malem spiritum conuertitur. Sic in vino est liquor Mercurialis diuersus à sale, qui ex tartaro siue sece vini efficitur. Idem quoque diuersus est à sulphure illo, quod in aqua ardente flammam concipit. Sic Mercurio rosarum cerebrum quasi recreatur. Sic suffimentis accommodatis cerebrum reficitur & recreatur. Non negamus vsuvenire vt animalis spiritus opprimatur siue intercipiatur aut à pituita: aut à sanguine: quocirca interdum venæ sectio in Apoplexia mirabiliter profuit: constat tamen Mercurium illum summum & præstantissimum: hoc est animalem spiritum Mercurio simili foueri, & à Mercurialibus excrementis obstruentibus, & aduersantibus laedi & pessundari. Sic vinū, licet calidum, morbos tamen gignit frigidos. Et quoniam nerui è cerebro prodeunt, & è medulla spinæ, quæ est cerebelli propago: perspicuū est Mercurios ὁμογενεῖς neruis prodesse: Verbi gratia: Mercurium castorei aut saluiae. Quinetiam princeps illa facultas intelligendi & ratiocinandi, cuius cerebrum est propria sedes, remediis ἀνλοις, & quouis Mercurio ψυχοπαμπωτικῷς, nempe accepta & hausta per aures auditione fœderis legis Dei, recreatur in sensum immortalem & vitam æternam: vt in Theologia demonstratum est. Postremo animaduertendum est, salem, qui est infimæ capacitatis, vt dictum est, tu cum media capacitate, hoc est cum thorace: tum etiam cum summa illa, hoc est cum capite communicari per venas tanquam per ductus & canaliculos quosdam. Sic quoniam pleuritis fit, quoties tenuibus costarum venis apertis aut disruptis, sanguis exiliens & collectus, inter costas & succingentem membranam phlegmonem parit: non absurdum fuerit venam secare, & tempore opportuno idoneoque, salem morbo accommodatum
units.tr: Paracelsus says this about investigating purgative medicines. Since this is so, it is clear that the most precise indications must be sought from that great Anatomy, whether the disease is to be treated or purged. Thus the heat of cassia fistula, the shape of the pod, and the seeds themselves digested in the pod indicate for which material they are prepared to be expelled. Likewise rhubarb has signs that indicate the signs of the material to be expelled [ἀντίσποφα]. Finally, there is no disease, whether it is similar (homoeomerous), organic, or a solution of continuity (that is, a common disease), whether a similar disease is solitary or accompanied by matter, provided that the disease is curable (for to heal the lame and the blind, for example, belongs to God alone). I say there is no disease that does not have its indication of remedy in that great Anatomy. Thus a wound made by a cut, which is a solution of continuity, has a counter-indication [ἀντίσπροφον] in androsaemum, whose crushed leaves exude a bloody juice, as Pliny teaches in book 27, chapter 4, and Dioscorides in book 3, chapters 146 and 148. Dioscorides says: St John's wort, rubbed between the fingers, releases a bloody juice, for which reason it is called androsaemon. And at the end of chapter 148 Dioscorides says: It checks blood in wounds. Therefore Paracelsus reproaches the common physicians for their ignorance of this most excellent Anatomy, in these words: Whenever our physicians treat a patient, he says, the whole business depends on luck. The foundation of their practice is that a sword makes a wound. Beyond that they know nothing. A sword certainly does not require medicine, but what does require it is nature, which they ignore; they know only the sword. The same Paracelsus, in many places concerning the great Anatomy, and at the end of the fourth treatise On the Method of Compounding Medicines, urges everyone in various words: The parents of man, he says, are heaven and earth. For this reason man was also born and grew in their nature and parts, apart from the image of God. Thus there is no separation here except of the image of God; nature remains inseparable from father and mother. Since, then, the parents of man are heaven and earth, from which the infant was finally created and learned from its parents, practise anatomy on the parents. Dissect them, not the children. When you have come to know heaven and earth you will have full knowledge of all human nature. So he speaks, and with these words he advises all physicians to seek the indications of remedies from that Anatomy. He adds the reason: because all the entelechies and forms of external remedies were created for man and refer to man, and they cannot be separated from matter, that is, from the earth from which those things were produced, no less than man himself. For God formed man from the earth. Therefore those forms are not separable [χωριστοὶ], that is, they cannot be separated from matter, whether they are considered in the lesser or the greater world. But the human soul alone is separable [χωριστὸς], that is, separable from matter, because it proceeded immediately from the breath of God breathed into the face of man, as we said in our demonstrative orations On the Separable Nature of the Human Soul and On the Resurrection of the Dead. Having thus explained these things, I come to the manner of use. In this manner of use one must consider the places through which the matter is to be expelled, or the medicine taken; the part to which remedies are to be applied; and likewise the time of the disease and the hour at which the remedies are to be used. Here, concerning the places through which the matter is to be expelled or the medicine taken, and likewise concerning the form of medicines, which according to Fernel is either liquid or solid, we shall say a little. There are three capacities in the temple of the human body, distinct from one another and separated by their places, which we have also touched upon briefly above. The lower belly, or lowest capacity, lies below the diaphragm, or below the transverse septum, and contains the stomach and the liver, from which the veins are drawn upward and downward; it also contains the spleen, kidneys, bladder, and womb. The middle capacity is that of the chest, containing the lungs and the heart, from which the arteries arise. The highest capacity is that which, as the highest sanctuary and as it were the place of oracles, constitutes the head, which we call the capacity of the head; it contains the brain and both membranes, whence also come the seven pairs of nerves. In it too lies the cerebellum, which is continued into the marrow of the spine, from which the other nerves arise. Now let us fit the forms of remedies to these three capacities. Salts suit the lowest capacity, which lies below the diaphragm, as has been said. Salt, like bread, meal, and chewed and softened food, is a solid form; and likewise a liquid form seems suited to the gullet, the stomach, and then the liver and spleen. So too clysters in liquid form suit the intestines. As for salts, salt seems to be opposed to salt. For example, in dropsy, where the liver's salt is dissolved, a salt that expels the dissolved salt must be given. Then a strengthening salt must be given. Thus in obstructions both of the liver and of the spleen, salts of such a kind must be given as will open the obstructions. And since salts seem suited to the liver, which is the parenchyma, or the viscus that produces blood, salts will also seem suited to the veins that proceed from the liver and to the parts of the body that are nourished by blood. Hence salt is also most suitable for fresh wounds, as is sugar. But the middle capacity, which is that of the chest, seems rather suited to the nature and form of those things that take fire, namely the nature of sulphur, oil, and theriacs, such as tragacanth and others of that kind. First, the middle capacity, on the side where it lies next to that highest capacity of the head, is helped by fumigations because of the lungs. Moreover, salt is not suited to fumigations, but sulphur is, as Dioscorides also teaches in book 5, chapter 73. Sulphur, says Dioscorides, benefits coughs, asthma, and those who expel pus, when taken in a single dose or as a fumigation. As for the fact that sugar and other salts, chosen suitably from the Anatomy, are usefully mixed with oil, for example fresh almond oil, and with theriacs, this happens because of the communication of the nature of salt through the vena cava, which runs upward through the diaphragm from the connection with the liver. Next, oil and butter, which, like sulphur and camphor, take fire, are similar to theriacs. Oils also, wisely chosen, are most suitable for anointing the chest, and likewise for protecting and guarding the region of the heart with ointment. Indeed, for that great light, namely the heart, which is as the sun in the lesser world, if its oil is not poured in, there is no doubt that the vital heat will be extinguished. Moreover, oil taken simply, like butter, and likewise fumigations from suitable oils and ointments, keep poisons away from the citadel of life. It must be observed, however, that there are different kinds of oils, whose powers and uses it is worth knowing distinctly, whether they are pressed from fruits, seeds, and kernels, or artificially extracted from salt. To the highest capacity, which is that of the head, the nature or substance of Mercury seems suited, which is far more perfect and far more elaborated than both salt and oil or sulphur. For the animal spirit, which is in the brain, and which flows through the channels of the nerves, both into the instruments of the senses and into the motor muscles, is first elaborated from the vital spirit, which is raised through the arteries of the neck into a wonderful network, says Fernel, and then in the inner second substance of the brain, which takes its name from the secondary parts, is converted by the innate power of the brain into the animal spirit. So in wine there is a mercurial liquor different from the salt that is produced from tartar or the lees of wine. It is also different from that sulphur which catches fire in brandy. So the brain, as it were, is refreshed by the Mercury of roses. So by suitable fumigations the brain is restored and revived. We do not deny that it sometimes happens that the animal spirit is oppressed or intercepted, either by phlegm or by blood; for this reason sometimes bloodletting has wonderfully helped in apoplexy. Yet it is established that that highest and most excellent Mercury, that is the animal spirit, is cherished by a similar Mercury, and is injured and destroyed by mercurial excrements that obstruct and oppose it. So wine, though hot, nonetheless produces cold diseases. And since the nerves arise from the brain and from the marrow of the spine, which is an offshoot of the cerebellum, it is clear that Mercuries that are homogeneous [ὁμογενεῖς] benefit the nerves: for example, the Mercury of castoreum or of sage. Moreover, that chief faculty of understanding and reasoning, whose proper seat is the brain, is revived by immaterial remedies [ἀνλοις] and by any soul-attracting Mercury [ψυχοπαμπωτικῷς], namely by the covenant of God's law received and drunk in through hearing, into immortal sense and eternal life, as has been shown in Theology. Finally, it must be noted that the salt of the lowest capacity, as has been said, communicates both with the middle capacity, that is with the thorax, and also with that highest capacity, that is with the head, through the veins as through certain channels and small canals. Thus, since pleurisy arises whenever the thin veins of the ribs are opened or broken, and the blood, escaping and collecting between the ribs and the enveloping membrane, produces an inflammation, it will not be absurd to open a vein, and at a suitable and opportune time to give a salt that is adapted to the disease.

units.la: E exhibere.Sic vtiles sunt reuulsiones, & deriuationes sanguinis, certis venis sectis: Verbi gratia: basilica secta, aut cephalica, dextri aut sinistri lateris siue cubiti.Item, malleoli secta a interiore, aut saphena.Eodem modo animaduertendum est, naturam sulphuris per Arterias communicari cum caeteris corporis partibus. Quo fit, vt Arteria vulnerata, sulphur & thus cum myrrha & aloe commodissimè adhibeantur. Sulphur enim, vt testis est Dioscorides, erumpentem undecunque sanguinem sistit. Sic etiam remedia illa, quae depromuntur è Mercurii Anatome, propter neruos, qui in totum corpus diducuntur, caeteris quoque partibus sunt salutaria. Eodem modo propter functiones partium primae regionis primò necessarias, Oesophagi, ventriculi, intestinorum purgationes, antegrediatur necesse est. Quidni enim antegrederentur? Erratum in prima concoctione, nō potest corrigi in progressu: vt rectè docent Auicenna & alii melii medici Arabes. Sic etiam in purgationibus vsu-venit. Erratū in purgatione primę regionis, incredibiles affert difficultates medendi. Ex his intelligimus, verissimum esse illud, quod in tractatu περὶ Δυσχημοσωνῆς Hippocrates ait: cum medendi scien tia coniunctam esse sapientiā & Dei cognitionem. : Itémque in medico inesse εἰδηοιν τῆς πρὸς βίον χρησῶν καὶ ἀ-ναγκαίων καθαρσίων. Atque haec de secundo capite, hoc est de accommodandis principiis Paracelsicis ad indicationes illas, quas medici sibi proponere solent.
units.tr: And to administer. Thus, derivations and revulsions of the blood are useful when certain veins are opened: for example, the basilic vein, or the cephalic, of the right or left arm or elbow. Likewise, the vein at the inner ankle (malleolus) or the saphena. In the same way we should observe that the nature of sulphur is communicated through the arteries to the other parts of the body. Hence, when an artery is wounded, sulphur and frankincense with myrrh and aloe are most suitably applied. For sulphur, as Dioscorides bears witness, checks blood breaking out from anywhere. Likewise, those remedies drawn from the anatomy of Mercury, because of the nerves which extend throughout the whole body, are also wholesome for the other parts. In the same way, because of the functions of the parts of the first region, which are necessary first, the purgings of the gullet, stomach and intestines must necessarily go before. Why should they not go before? An error in the first concoction cannot be corrected in the course of the treatment: as Avicenna and the other more sound Arab physicians rightly teach. The same thing happens with purgations too: an error in purging the first region brings with it incredible difficulties in healing. From these things we understand that what Hippocrates says in his treatise On Decorum is most true: that wisdom and knowledge of God are joined with the science of healing, and that a physician ought to possess a knowledge of the purgations that are useful and necessary for life [εἰδήσιν τῆς πρὸς βίον χρησίμων καὶ ἀναγκαίων καθαρσίων]. And so much for the second chapter, that is, on adapting the Paracelsian principles to those indications which physicians are accustomed to set before themselves.

units.la: Tertium & postremum caput erit de lapide illo admirabili. Ante omnia, utrum lapis ille admirabilis, quem philosophicum vocant, sit necne quaerendum est. Hoc ipsum quaerere, nihil aliud est, quàm quaerere: Vtrum in lapide illo rubro, praeparato eo modo quo praeparandum esse docent Alchymistæ, insit vis illa transmutandi metalla in aurum, necne?Itémque,vtrum in lapide candido illo insit vis transmutandi cætera præter aurum, metalla in argentum, necne? Scimus quidem aurum esse:itémque argentum esse:sed vtrum vis illa transmutandi, insit in illis lapidibus necne, nondum compertum est.Atqui oportuit ante compertum esse,vim illam transmutandi,inesse in lapidibus illis,quàm quæreremus, quidnam sit causa, quamobrem lapis ex auro transmutet cætera metalla in aurum:itémq;, quamobrem lapis ex argento,transmutet cætera metalla in argentum. Sic nisi compertum esset nobis, esse eclipsim lunæ: ὅτι ἔσην:non quæreremus Διότι:quamobrem fit eclipsis lunæ: siue quæ causa sit eclipseos lunæ. Proinde auaritiam incredibilé producunt ineptissimi homines, quicunq; ad χρυσοποιίαν istam ante aggrediuntur,quàm sciant ὅτι ἔστι. Atqui dicent sibi compertum esse: lapidem ad aurum: itémque lapidem ad argentum esse.Respondemus: etiamsi concedamus mus esse lapides istiusmodi, nos tamen pernaegare, in istiusmodi lapidibus inesse vim transmutandi & conuertendi cætera metalla in aurum & argetum. Esto subiectū: lapis præparatus ad aurū. Attributum esto: potest transmutare cætera metalla in aurum. Item: esto subiectum: lapis præparatus ad argentum. Attributum esto: potest transmutare siue conuertere inferiora metalla in argentum. Aio: neque attributum hoc posse tribui lapidi ad argentum: neq; illud lapidi ad aurum. Fatemur quidem lapidū istorum accuratissimè præparatorum partes adeo misceri cum minutissimis quibusque partibus eius metallifusi, in quod iniiciūtur, vt fiat quasi crama quoddam metallicum. Etenim si metallum nihil aliud est, quam aqua terrea multo frigore congelata: quæ propterea non nisi multo calore restitui potest in pristinum fluore; non est mirum aurum & argentum posse fieri vnum per crasim: præsertim quum puluis auri accuratissimè praeparatus in argentum fusum proiicitur. Ergo fit vnum per crasim: nō autem vnum per generationē. Proin de forma auri remanet in materia, & in partibus auri, vt & forma argenti remanet in materia argenti: non secus atque in cramate, id est, in vino cum aqua, remanet vtriusque, nempe vini & aquae forma. Alio etiā modo ὅπ ἐϛ) probare & demonstrare conantur æruscatores isti, ex Paracelso. Rustici in Hungaria, inquit Paracelsus, cum ferrum suo tempore proiiciunt in fontem quendam vulgari nomine Zipffer brunnen, in ferruginem consumitur, quae follibus & igne liquefacta, mox pura Venus existit, quae nunquam in ferrum amplius redit. Similiter in monte Kuttenberg vulgariter nuncupato, capitellum aut lixiuium ex Marchasitis colant, in quo ferrum etiā in optimā venere trāsit altè gradatā, & malleo tractabiliore altera naturali. Hęc Paracelsus: quorum etiamsi fidē nobis facias, mi Vencislae, nihilominus alias demōstrationes ὅπ requiremus. Neque que enim nos qui Apodicticè tractandi rationem cum Aristotele tradimus, in istiusmodi probationibus acquiescimus. Alio etiam modo ὅτι ἐςὶ probare conantur. Ex minio, inquiunt, fit argentum viuum. Sic Dioscorides: argentum viuum, inquit, fit ex minio, quod abusiuè cinnabaris dicitur, patinis fictilibus impositaferrea concha cinnabarim continente, & calice cooperta, argilla superlita, carbonibus succendunt. Siquidem detersa fuligo, quae calici insidet, refrigerata in argentum viuum coit. Haec Dioscorides. Sic etiam ex aqua salsa aiunt artificiosè fieri salem. Ex quibus concludunt, similiter quoque ex argento, adhibito artificio, posse fieri aurum.
units.tr: The third and last chapter will concern that wonderful stone. Above all, we must ask whether that admirable stone, which they call philosophical, exists or not. To ask this is nothing other than to ask: Whether in that red stone, prepared in the way that the alchemists teach it must be prepared, there is that power of transmuting metals into gold, or not? Likewise: whether in that white stone there is the power of transmuting the other metals, apart from gold, into silver, or not? We indeed know that gold exists, and that silver exists; but whether that power of transmuting is in those stones or not has not yet been established. Yet it ought to have been established beforehand that that power of transmuting is in those stones, before we asked what is the cause why the stone from gold transmutes the other metals into gold, and likewise why the stone from silver transmutes the other metals into silver. So, unless we knew that there is an eclipse of the moon [ὅτι ἔστιν], we would not ask why [Διότι] an eclipse of the moon happens, or what the cause of the lunar eclipse is. Therefore the most foolish men, who take up that goldmaking [χρυσοποιίαν] before they know that it is [ὅτι ἔστι], produce an incredible greed. But they will say that it is known to them that there is a stone for gold and likewise a stone for silver. We reply: even if we grant that stones of this kind exist, we nonetheless flatly deny that in such stones there is the power of transmuting and converting the other metals into gold and silver. Let the subject be: a stone prepared for gold. Let the predicate be: it can transmute the other metals into gold. Likewise: let the subject be a stone prepared for silver; let the predicate be it can transmute or convert the inferior metals into silver. I say that this predicate cannot be attributed to the stone for silver, nor that one to the stone for gold. We do grant that the parts of those stones, most accurately prepared, mix so intimately with the tiniest parts of the molten metal into which they are cast that a sort of metallic mixture (crama) results. For if metal is nothing other than watery earth congealed by great cold, which therefore cannot be restored to its former fluidity except by great heat, it is no wonder that gold and silver can become one by mixture, especially when powder of gold, most carefully prepared, is thrown into molten silver. So it becomes one by mixture, but not one by generation. Therefore the form of gold remains in the matter and in the parts of gold, just as the form of silver remains in the matter of silver; just as in a mixture, that is, in wine with water, the form of each remains, namely of wine and of water. These tinkers also try to prove and demonstrate that it is [ὅτι ἔστι] in another way, from Paracelsus. Peasants in Hungary, says Paracelsus, when at the proper time they throw iron into a certain spring called by the common name Zipffer brunnen, it is consumed into rust, which, melted by bellows and fire, soon becomes pure Venus, which never returns into iron again. Similarly on the mountain commonly called Kuttenberg, they strain a lye or still-liquor from marcasites, in which iron also passes into the finest Venus, raised to a high grade, and with a more workable malleability than the natural kind. Thus Paracelsus. Even if you were to make us believe these things, my Wenceslas, we would nonetheless require other demonstrations that it is [ὅτι]. For we, who hand down the method of demonstrative reasoning with Aristotle, do not rest content with proofs of this kind. They also try to prove that it is [ὅτι ἐστί] in another way. From minium, they say, quicksilver is made. So Dioscorides: quicksilver, he says, is made from minium, which is improperly called cinnabar: placed on earthen dishes, with an iron bowl containing the cinnabar, covered with a lid and smeared over with clay, they set it alight with charcoal. For the soot that clings to the lid, once cleaned off and cooled, comes together into quicksilver. Thus Dioscorides. So too they say that salt is artificially made from salt water. From these things they conclude that in the same way gold can be made from silver by art.

units.la: Respondemus: ex minio sive cinnabari artificiosè posse fieri argentum viuum: itémque ex aqua salsa, salé: nepe: quia sal est in aqua salsa: itémque argentum viuum in minio: sed aurum non esse similiter in argento: ac propterea ex argento non posse fieri aurum. Reperti sunt tandem, qui dixerunt lapidem istum veteribus il lis cognitum fuisse, quippe cuius Hippocrates mentionem fecerit in Epistola ad Crateuam his verbis,τὸ ἡ χρῆμα τῆς ζοταν̃ων, παρά σοι πολλάκις ἐ- θωύμασα. ὡς ἢ τὴν ὅλωνγε φύσιν τε ἢ δια- ταξιν, ἡ τὸ ἱερώτατον γῆς ἵδρυμα. ἐξ ἧς τὰ ζῶα, ἡ φυτά, ἡ τροφαὶ, ἡ φάρμακα, ἡ τύχη, ἡ ὁ πλοῦτος αὐτὸς ἀναφύεται. ἃ ἢ γὰρ ἂν εἴ- χεν οἱ ἐπιδη̃, ἡ φιλαργυρίη. οὐ δ' ἂν Ἀβδη- ρίται μὲν νεῦ δέκα τοσαύτοις ἐδελέαζον, ἀντὶ ἵντρε μισθωτὸν ἐλέγχοντες. id est: At vero rem herbariam apud te, persæpe sum admi- ratus sicut etiam vniuersorum naturam & dispositionem: & constitutum sacrarium terræ, ex qua animalia, plantæ, & alimen- ta, & medicamenta, & fortuna, & ipsæ di- uitiæ exoriuntur. Nequæ enim, quo conce- deret, auaritia haberet. Neque Abderitæ me decem talētis nūc inescarēt, pro medico mer- cenariū declarantes. Hęc, in Epistola ad Crateuā. Sed vt nihil dicā de morosis criticis, qui fortasse negabunt Epistolam hanc esse Hippocratis: videntur verba hæc detorqueri in alienū sensum, sum, quum de lapide illo accipiuntur & intelliguntur. Quis enim non videt describi sacrarium quoddam, & quasi penetrales quasdam (cabinet nostri vocant) in quibus vniversitatis natura sit depicta & quasi repræsentata. Deinde, non video, quo pacto verba hæc: (Neque enim, quo se reciperet, auaritia haberet, &c. cum superioribus cohæreant. Denique istiusmodi authoritates, quas vocant, non sunt demonstrationes ὅτι, neque definitiones ὅτι. Atqui ante omnia demonstrandum est ὅτι εςι. deinde διότι: vt in posterioribus Analyticis docuimus. Sunt alii, qui neruosius probare & argumentari conentur. Aiunt enim lapide illum admirabilem, siue philosophicum, esse tanquam acetum, aut fermentum. Quemadmodum enim in aceto est vis transmutandi siue conuertendi vinum in acetum: & in fermento vis conuertendi massam in fermentum: ita etiam in lapide illo inesse vim conuertendi & transmutandi. Sic igitur isti conantur probare ὅτι ἐςὶ: hoc est, non esse ficta & comentitia vim couertendi & transmu tandi, quā lapidi illi admirabili tribuūt. Pri mū animaduertendū est, nihil aliud effici ista argumētatione, quā reperi ri in natura rerū quaedā, quae praedita sint vi trāsmutādi & cōuertēdi in suā naturā. Quod si ita esse in aceto & fer mento cōpertū est nobis, nō sequitur cōpertū esse nobis, vim simile inesse in lapide illo admirabili. Neq; enim aurum est res corrupta, vt est acetum. Voco rem corruptam, illud quod est κατὰ στέρησιν ἡ κατὰ φθορὰν τὴν πρὸς φύ-σιν: id est, quod ex priuatione & cor-ruptione praeter naturā existit: cui op ponitur τὸ κατ' ἕξιν ἡ κατὰ τὸ εἶδος. Sic τὸ εἶδος, acetum, est res κατὰ στέρησιν καὶ κατὰ φθορὰν τὴν πρὸς φύσιν. Iccirco ace-tum non potest reuerti in naturam vini, tantùm abest vt acetum prædi-tum sit vi conuertendi in vinum. Sic Aristoteles libro septimo primae phi losophiae, qui liber latinis est octa-uus, negat vinum esse potestate acetum: sed, quod ad aquâ attinet, aquâ esse potestate acetum & vinum. Τὸ ὕδωρ, inquit, δύναμει ὄξος καὶ οἶνος. τῇ μὲν, καθ' ἓξιν ἡ κατὰ τὸ εἶδος, ὕλη. τῇ ἡ, κατὰ στέρησιν ἡ κατὰ φθοράν τὴν παρὰ φύσιν: id est: acetum & vinum sunt potestate aqua: ac huius quidem, nempe vini, ratione habitus & formæ, aqua est materia: illius autem, nempe aceti, aqua est materia ratione corruptionis eius quæ præter naturam est. Atqui lapis ille philosophicus, qui argentum, Verbi gratia, transmutat in aurum, non est res corrupta, eo modo, quo acetum.
units.tr: We reply: from minium or cinnabar, quicksilver can be artificially made; likewise salt from salt water, namely because salt is in salt water, and quicksilver is in minium; but gold is not similarly in silver, and therefore gold cannot be made from silver. Some have at last been found who say that this stone was known to the ancients, since Hippocrates mentioned it in his Epistle to Crateuas in these words: [Τὸ δὲ χρῆμα τὸ ἐρβόριον παρά σοι πολλάκις ἐθαύμασα, ὡς ἢ τὴν ὅλων γε φύσιν τε καὶ διάταξιν, ἢ τὸ ἱερώτατον γῆς ἵδρυμα, ἐξ ἧς τὰ ζῷα, ἢ φυτά, ἢ τροφαὶ, ἢ φάρμακα, ἢ τύχη, ἢ ὁ πλοῦτος αὐτὸς ἀναφύεται. ἃ ἢ γὰρ ἂν εἶχεν οἱ ἐπιδοῦναι, ἢ φιλαργυρίη. οὐδ' ἂν Ἀβδηρῖται μὲν νῦν δέκα τοσαύτοις ἐδελέαζον, ἀντὶ ἰητροῦ μισθωτὸν ἐλέγχοντες.] That is: "But I have often admired the herbal matter with you, as well as the nature and arrangement of the whole, and the most sacred foundation of the earth, from which animals, plants, foods, medicines, fortune, and wealth itself spring up. For avarice would have nothing to give in return for these things. Nor would the Abderites now lure me with ten talents, declaring me a mercenary instead of a physician." So far the Epistle to Crateuas. But, to say nothing of the fussy critics who will perhaps deny that this Epistle is Hippocrates', these words seem to be twisted into a foreign sense when they are taken and understood of that stone. For who does not see that a certain sacred place is being described, and as it were inner chambers (which we call a cabinet), in which the nature of the universe is depicted and, as it were, represented? Next, I do not see how these words, For avarice would have nothing to give in return, etc., cohere with what precedes. Finally, authorities of this kind, as they are called, are not demonstrations that it is [ὅτι], nor definitions that it is. Yet above all it must be demonstrated that it is [ὅτι ἔστι], and then why [διότι], as we taught in the Posterior Analytics. There are others who try to prove and argue more vigorously. For they say that that admirable or philosophical stone is like vinegar or leaven. For just as in vinegar there is the power of transmuting or converting wine into vinegar, and in leaven the power of converting a mass into leaven, so too in that stone there is the power of converting and transmuting. Thus they try to prove that it is [ὅτι ἐστί]: that is, that the power of converting and transmuting, which they attribute to that admirable stone, is not feigned or invented. First, it must be noted that this argument achieves nothing more than showing that there are certain things in nature endowed with the power of transmuting and converting into their own nature. But if it has been established for us that this is so in vinegar and leaven, it does not follow that it has been established for us that a similar power is in that admirable stone. For gold is not a corrupted thing, as vinegar is. By a corrupted thing I mean that which exists by privation and corruption contrary to nature, that is, which arises from privation and corruption beyond nature, and which is opposed to what exists according to habit or according to form. Thus vinegar, as a species, is a thing that exists by privation and by corruption contrary to nature. Hence vinegar cannot revert to the nature of wine; so far is vinegar from being endowed with the power of converting into wine. So Aristotle, in book seven of the First Philosophy (which is book eight in the Latin division), denies that wine is potentially vinegar, but says that, as regards water, water is potentially both vinegar and wine. [Τὸ ὕδωρ δύναμει ὄξος καὶ οἶνος. τῇ μὲν καθ' ἕξιν ἢ κατὰ τὸ εἶδος ὕλη, τῇ δὲ κατὰ στέρησιν ἢ κατὰ φθορὰν τὴν παρὰ φύσιν.] That is: "Acetum and wine are potentially water; and water is the matter of the one according to habit or form, namely of wine, and of the other, namely of vinegar, according to privation or the corruption that is contrary to nature." But that philosophical stone, which transmutes silver, for example, into gold, is not a corrupted thing in the way vinegar is.

units.la: Nam si esset res corrupta eo modo, quo est acetum, non posset reuerti ad aurum: nedum argentum conuer teret in aurum. Quinetiam si esset res corrupta, eo modo, quo est acetum: citius ex Mercurio illo vulgari, (siquidem Mercurius ille vulgaris est aqua & materia metallorum, quàm ex re corrupta præter naturam) aurū efficeretur, non secus atque ex aqua vinum citius efficiatur, quâ ex aceto vinum. Sic Ariftoteles: ἡ τῆ ζωὴ ὕλη, αὐτὴ καταφθορᾷ νεκρᾶ δυνάμεις καὶ ὕλη, ἡ τὸ ὕδωρ ὄξεος. γίγνεται γὰρ ἐν τέττων ὥσπερ ἐξ ἡμέρας νύξ. ἡ ὅσα δὴ ἕτω μεταβάλλει εἰς ἄλληλα, εἰς τὴν ὕλην δεῖ ἐπανελθεῖν.Ipsa animalis materia, etiã eius, quod per corruptionem & interitum cadauer est, potestas & materia est.Sic etiam aqua aceti potestas & materia est. Ista enim fiunt ex illis,non secus atque ex die fit nox. Sic etiã omnia illa in materiam reuerti oportet, quorumcunque mutua est transmutatio. Hæc Ariftoteles. Non est igitur lapis philosophicus vt acetum. Nam si esset vt acetum, esset res corrupta & præter naturam, quæ rem naturalē certa mensura admixtam corrumperet & in rem non naturalem transmutaret. Sic vinum, certa mensura, hoc est, nō nimium, admixtum aceto, (nam si largius affundatur, aceti vis elanguescit) corrumpitur, & in acetum conuertitur atque transmutatur. Non disputo hîc, vtrum subitò vinum conuertatur in acetum, necne. Hoc solū dico & affirmo cum Aristotele, materiam, Verbi gratia, Mercurium illum vulgarem, si est materia metallorum, esse potestate aurum: at ex lapide philosophico, si est vt acetum, aurum nullo modo posse fieri. Quan doquidem enim acetum est res corrupta, & præter naturam, cum acetū conuertit vinum in suam naturam, non generat vinum, sed corrumpit & perdit. Ergo lapis philosophicus, non est vt acetum, sed vt materia. Verbi gratia: est vt aqua, quæ est materia vini & aceti. Quod si est vt materia: profecto in lapide philosophico non erit vis transmutandi. Nam materia est ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως, non autem τῆς κινεῖν: hoc est, principium quamobrem res moueatur: non autem, quamobrem moueat, siue, est principium passiuū, non autem actiuū, vt vulgo loquuntur. Exempli gratia. Aqua nunquam ipsa se transmutauerit in vinum, nisi accedat principium mutans, quod quidem principium mutans sit naturale.Sic etiam aqua,siue materia, nō dederit eam formam, quam non habet. Exempli gratia. Aqua non dederit vini formam,quam non habet. Quod si in lapide philosophico non inest vis conuertendi siue transmutandi: multò minùs inerit vis multiplicādi,post primam proiectionem: quam tamen multiplicandi vim, lapidi isti omnes tribuunt.Huius fermenti, inquiunt, multiplicatio notanda est, ad hunc neꝛupe modum. Soluatur in humido suo: postmodum ad regimen ignis ponatur vt priùs,& aget in suam humiditatem citiùs quàm antea: necnon transmutabit in suam substantiam: non secus ac parum fermenti magnam farinæ quantitatem videtur in fermentum trāsmutare totam. Quapropter ineffabilis est in terris thesaurus, cui mundus parem non habet, Augurello teste, &c. Cæterùm quæ de aceto dicta sunt, etiam ad fermentum transferri possunt. Fermentum enim est tanquam massa corrupta: non secus atque acetum est vinum corruptum.
units.tr: For if it were a corrupt thing in the way vinegar is, it could not be turned back into gold, much less convert silver into gold. Moreover, if it were a corrupt thing in the way vinegar is, gold would be produced more quickly from that common Mercury (since that common Mercury is water and the matter of metals, not a thing corrupted against nature), just as wine is produced more quickly from water than from vinegar. Thus Aristotle: [ἡ τῆ ζωὴ ὕλη, αὐτὴ καταφθορᾷ νεκρᾶ δυνάμεις καὶ ὕλη, ἡ τὸ ὕδωρ ὄξεος. γίγνεται γὰρ ἐν τέττων ὥσπερ ἐξ ἡμέρας νύξ. ἡ ὅσα δὴ ἕτω μεταβάλλει εἰς ἄλληλα, εἰς τὴν ὕλην δεῖ ἐπανελθεῖν.] The very matter of an animal, even of that which through corruption and death becomes a corpse, is potency and matter. So also the water of vinegar is potency and matter. For these come from those, just as night comes from day. So all things that change into one another must return to matter, whatever their mutual transmutation may be. So Aristotle. Therefore the philosophers' stone is not like vinegar. For if it were like vinegar, it would be a corrupt thing contrary to nature, which, when mixed in a certain measure with a natural thing, would corrupt it and transform it into something unnatural. Thus wine, when mixed in a certain measure with vinegar (that is, not too much, for if it is poured in more freely the strength of the vinegar weakens), is corrupted and turned and transformed into vinegar. I do not here dispute whether wine is suddenly converted into vinegar or not. This alone I say and affirm with Aristotle: the matter, for example that common Mercury, if it is the matter of metals, is gold potentially; but if the philosophers' stone were like vinegar, gold could in no way be made from it. For since vinegar is a corrupt thing and contrary to nature, when it converts wine into its own nature, it does not generate wine but corrupts and destroys it. Therefore the philosophers' stone is not like vinegar but like matter. For example, it is like water, which is the matter of wine and of vinegar. But if it is like matter, then surely there will be no power of transmuting in the philosophers' stone. For matter is the principle of motion [ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως], not of moving [τῆς κινεῖν]: that is, the principle by which a thing is moved, not that by which it moves; or it is a passive principle, not an active one, as people commonly put it. For example: water will never change itself into wine unless a changing principle, which is natural, comes to it. Likewise water, or matter, will not give that form which it does not have. For example, water will not give the form of wine, which it does not have. But if there is no power of converting or transmuting in the philosophers' stone, there will much less be a power of multiplying after the first projection; yet all these men attribute to that stone a power of multiplying. The multiplication of this leaven, they say, is to be noted, in this manner: let it be dissolved in its moisture; then let it be placed over the fire regulated as before, and it will work into its moisture more quickly than before, and will also transmute into its own substance; just as a little leaven seems to transmute a great quantity of flour entirely into leaven. Therefore there is an ineffable treasure on earth, to which the world has no equal, as Augurellus testifies, etc. Moreover, what has been said of vinegar can also be applied to leaven. For leaven is like a corrupt mass, just as vinegar is corrupted wine.

units.la: Sic in sacris,fermentum & fermenti expers opponuntur. An nescitis, inquit Apostolus, paululo fermenti totam massam fermentari? Expurgate igitur vetus fermentum, ut sitis nova massa, sicut estis fermenti expertes. Postremò, quod quidam aiunt, lapidem istum admirabilem esse semen auri:
units.tr: Thus in the sacred writings, leaven and that which is free of leaven are set against each other. Do you not know, says the Apostle, that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. Finally, as some say, this admirable stone is the seed of gold:

units.la: (in auro
units.tr: (in gold

units.la: Semina sunt auri, inquit ille, quamvis abstrusa recedant Longius, & multo nobis quaerenda labore.) facilè refelli potest. Neq; enim Deus opt.max. quum vniuersum hoc condidit, vt stirpibus, & aliis eiusmodi, ita etiam auro indidit semen. Neque sunt auri rami, in quibus sint taleae, vt sunt oleae rami, in quibus sunt multae taleae. Ergo lapis admirabilis dicitur semen metaphoricè. Atqui neque definiendum, neque demonstrandum est metaphoris. Nam metaphorae confundunt genera & species: quae confusio in demõstrationibus summopere vitanda est. ἐὰν ᾖ μὴ ἀλλήγεσις.
units.tr: Seeds of gold are there, he says, though they lie hidden far off and must be sought with much labour.) This can easily be refuted. For God, the best and greatest, when he made this universe, did not implant seed in gold as he did in plants and things of that kind. Nor are there branches of gold on which shoots are found, as olive branches have many shoots. Therefore the admirable stone is called seed metaphorically. But a metaphor is neither to be defined nor to be demonstrated. For metaphors confuse genera and species, and such confusion must be greatly avoided in demonstrations. [ἐὰν ᾖ μὴ ἀλλήγεσις.]

units.la: δεῖ μεταφορὰς, δῆλον ὅτι ἐὰν ὁρίζεσθαι, ὅτε μεταφορὰς. διαλέγεσθαι γὰρ ἀναγκὴν ἔσαι μεταφορᾶς.id est: si non oportet disputare metaphoris: perspicuum est, neque Metaphoris definiendum esse, neque definienda esse illa, quæcunque metaphoris exprimuntur: inquit Aristoteles. Et quoniam omnes scientiæ definitione constituuntur: (ut docet idem Aristoteles. Πάσαι αἱ ἐπιστῆμαι δι' ὁρισμῶν γίνονται, inquit:) Cùmque notionis omnis ianua & vestibulum sit definitio ἐννοηματικὴ, quam Galenus ὀνοματώδη appellat: siquidem definitio ἐννοηματικὴ lapidis philosophici à nemine adhuc tradi potuit: necesse est causas δίοτι lapidis admirabilis à nemine adhuc exponi potuisse. Nam definitio ἐννοηματικὴ nos docet ὅτι ἐςί. Sic, ubi scimus, eclipsim lunæ esse privationè lucis illius, quâ luna accipit à sole, quâdo quidè hac definitione ἐννοηματικὴ scimus ὅτι ἐςί: tu recte perquirimus διότι. Cur luna privatur luce illa, quâ accipere solet à Sole? Nempe, quia terra κατὰ διάμετρον interponitur inter inter Solem & lunam. τὸ ζητεῖν τί ἐστι, μὴ ἐ- χοντας ὅτι ἐστὶ, μηδὲν ζητεῖν ἐστι.id est.Quaere, quidnam sit res: hoc est, rei causas διότι perquirere, quum utrum res sit necne, ignores, prorsus est nihil quaerere. Afferant saltem definitionem ςυνομματικὴν lapidis philosophici: hoc est, doceant nos ὅτι ἐστι: tum causas perquiremus, scientiámque illam ad praecepta τρόπως ἀπαιδεύσιας dirigemus. Ex iis quae adhuc dicta sunt, intelligimus, aurum factitium, nihil aliud esse quam crama metallicum: quemadmodum etiam initio huius tertii capitis dictum est. Iccirco lapidi isti vim tingendi non alia ratione tribuit Paracelsus, quàm si fiat crama. Si tinctura tingere debet, inquit, necesse est corpus vel materiam quae tingenda est, apertam esse & influxu stare & nisi hoc fieret: tinctura operari non posset. Nam fieret sicut si quis crocum vel alium colorem in aquam coagulatam vel glaciem proiiceret: ita enim non tam cito glaciem suo colore tingeret, ac si in aliam aquam proiiceretur: & quamvis tingeret, simul tamen glaciem in aquam resolueret. Quare etiam metalla, quæ tingere volumus, in igni liquefieri oportet, & à sua coagulatione liberari: & hic sciendum est, quòd quo calidius liquescunt, eò celerius ea tinctura transcurrit: sicut fermetum penetrat, & totam massam acetositate inficit: Et quò melius obuelatur, quoque calidiùs custoditur massa, eò melius fermentat, & eò meliorem panem dat. Est enim fermentum tinctura massæ farinaceæ & panis. Et paulò post. Tincturas metallorum (inquit) necesse est esse naturæ fixæ fluxibilis, & incombustibilis: ita ut si parum eius laminæ metallicæ ignitæ iniiciatur, mox sicut cera fluat, idque sine omni fumo, metallúmque penetret vt oleum papyrum, vel aqua spongiam, omniaque metalla in album & rubrum tingant: hoc est in lunam & Solem.
units.tr: Aristotle: If one must not dispute by means of metaphors, it is clear that neither should metaphors be defined, nor should the things expressed by metaphors be defined. [δεῖ μεταφορὰς, δῆλον ὅτι ἐὰν ὁρίζεσθαι, ὅτε μεταφορὰς. διαλέγεσθαι γὰρ ἀναγκὴν ἔσαι μεταφορᾶς.] And since all sciences are constituted by definition (as the same Aristotle teaches; he says: [Πάσαι αἱ ἐπιστῆμαι δι' ὁρισμῶν γίνονται]), and since the gate and vestibule of all understanding is the notional definition [ἐννοηματικὴ], which Galen calls verbal [ὀνοματώδη]; since a notional definition of the philosophers' stone has not yet been given by anyone, it is necessary that the causes of the admirable stone [διότι] have not yet been set out by anyone. For a notional definition teaches us that a thing is [ὅτι ἐςί]. So when we know, that the eclipse of the moon is the privation of that light which the moon receives from the sun, we know by this notional definition that it is [ὅτι ἐςί]; then we rightly ask why [διότι]. Why is the moon deprived of that light which it is wont to receive from the Sun? Namely, because the earth is interposed diametrically between the Sun and the moon. [τὸ ζητεῖν τί ἐστι, μὴ ἔχοντας ὅτι ἐστὶ, μηδὲν ζητεῖν ἐστι.] That is: Seek what a thing is; that is, to seek the causes of a thing [διότι], while you do not know whether the thing is or not, is altogether to seek nothing. Let them at least set out a notional definition [ςυνομματικὴν] of the philosophers' stone: that is, let them teach us that it is [ὅτι ἐστι]; then we will inquire into the causes and direct that science to precepts [τρόπως ἀπαιδεύσιας]. From what has been said so far we understand that artificial gold is nothing other than a metallic crama, as was also said at the beginning of this third chapter. Therefore Paracelsus attributes to that stone the power of tinting only on the ground that it is made into a crama. If a tincture ought to tint, he says, it is necessary that the body or matter which is to be tinted be open and yielding to influx; and unless this happened, the tincture could not work. For it would be as if someone threw saffron or another colour into coagulated water or ice: thus it would not tint the ice with its colour as quickly as if it were thrown into other water; and although it would tint it, nonetheless it would dissolve the ice into water. Hence the metals we wish to tint must also be liquefied in fire and freed from their coagulation. And here it must be known that the more hotly they melt, the more quickly the tincture passes through them, just as leaven penetrates and infects the whole mass with its sourness; and the better the mass is covered and the more warmly it is kept, the better it ferments and the better bread it gives. For leaven is the tincture of the floury mass and of bread. And a little later: The tinctures of metals, he says, must be of a fixed, fluid and incombustible nature, so that if a little of it is thrown on heated metal plate, it will immediately flow like wax, and without any smoke, and penetrate the metal as oil penetrates paper or water a sponge, and tinge all metals white and red, that is, into the Moon and the Sun.

units.la: HÆC HABVI, quæ ad te, VENCISLAE LAVINI, de tribus illis capitibus initio propositis perscribe-rem.
units.tr: Here is what I have written to you, Wenceslas Lavinius, concerning those three points proposed at the beginning.

units.la: Primùm breuiter docuimus Anatomen illam præstantissimam discenscendam & cognoscędam esse ex si-gnus: signa esse similia atque ἀντίςροφα tum in eo subiecto, quod morbo af-sectum est, tum etiam in remedio: si-gna posita esse in coloribus, figuris, & proprijs accidentibus aliis: Eadem rectè appellari ὑπάρχοντα, ac proinde ad cō stituendum physiognomicum syl-logismum esse colligenda & adhi-benda. Deinde in secundo capite Anato-men illam præstantissimam reuocandam esse ad tria illa consequentia & principia summè vniuersalia, quę salem sulphur, Mercurium appelles, per me licet. Sic enim constare nobis Anatomes illius propemodum immensæ Epi-tomen maximè necessariam, ad quā etiam indicationes commodissimè di-rigi possint. Postremò de lapide illo admi-rabili, ὅτι ἐςι, nondū compertū esse dixim9: ac propterea frustra perquiri τὸ διότι, & causas eius, quod vtrum sit necne, ignoramus. Reliquum est, vt hæc o-mnia, diligenter expendas: mihíque super his sententiam tuam vicissim
units.tr: First, I briefly showed that this most excellent anatomy is to be learned and understood from signs, and that the signs are correlative [ἀντίστροφα] both in the subject affected by the disease and in the remedy. The signs lie in colours, figures, and other proper accidents. These are rightly called inherent qualities [ὑπάρχοντα], and so they must be gathered and applied to construct the physiognomic syllogism. Next, I said that in the second chapter this most excellent anatomy must be traced back to those three consequent and most universal principles, which you may call salt, sulphur and mercury, if you like. For in this way we would have an epitome of that almost immense anatomy, which is most necessary, and to which the indications can also be most conveniently directed. Lastly, I said that concerning that wonderful stone, whether it is [ὅτι ἐστι] is not yet known, so that the why [τὸ διότι] and its causes are sought in vain, since we do not know whether it is or not. It remains for you to weigh all these things carefully and to send me your opinion on them in return.
